#22531. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2516 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance.
  • How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.
  • Sources indicate that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a upcoming fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Sources indicate that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a upcoming fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my big shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

After finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

“I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev stated, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

According to recent reports, “Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he mentioned. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

“There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the prepares because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

According to recent reports, “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that plan. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

Sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

In a recent development, “It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

And for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

“To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

According to recent reports, “You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

Sources indicate that it worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

It has been revealed that “I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before significant races.”.

In a recent development, the day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

Industry observers note that “When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

Recent findings suggest that “I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

According to recent reports, that feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

“It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

According to recent reports, thankfully for him, time went by rapidly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

Industry observers note that after that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

Recent findings suggest that recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

It has been revealed that starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a upcoming world’s best time, the specter of the Massive Island tempered his elation.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his latest, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev promptly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of upcoming cooling strategy.

“It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

Industry observers note that when you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

It has been revealed that “We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev promptly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

Recent findings suggest that “My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

Industry observers note that for now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

Recent findings suggest that “Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

Sources indicate that “He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

#22530. 10 Ways to Strengthen Your Overlooked Arm Muscles in Yoga

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1409 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

10 Ways to Strengthen Your Overlooked Arm Muscles in Yoga

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, longtime yoga teacher Amber Burke, graduate of two YogaWorks teacher trainings and former leader of a teacher training program at the University of New Mexico-Taos, shares some of her favorite yoga arm strength exercises.
  • Have you ever walked out of yoga class with noodle arms?
  • In a recent development, yet there are plenty of yoga poses that could strengthen these muscles of the arms if you know how to adapt them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, longtime yoga teacher Amber Burke, graduate of two YogaWorks teacher trainings and former leader of a teacher training program at the University of New Mexico-Taos, shares some of her favorite yoga arm strength exercises. You can also explore other ways to strengthen your arms in yoga.

Have you ever walked out of yoga class with noodle arms? That’s likely because a typical vinyasa class, with its repeated Planks, Downward Dogs, and arm balances, works your chest, fronts of your shoulders, and triceps—aka, the muscles responsible for “pushing” movements. So much so, it’s become a truism that yoga tends to overlook the “pull” muscles, including those of the upper back, backs of your shoulders, biceps, and forearms.

In a recent development, yet there are plenty of yoga poses that could strengthen these muscles of the arms if you know how to adapt them. In poses that usually allow your arms to rest, you can strengthen your underutilized muscles by creating a little resistance.

The following poses engage muscles that your usual yoga class might overlook. Bonus: In many of these, your legs are working a little harder, too, as your lower body supplies an opposing force for the arms. No gym or weights required. Although you will need a strap or belt and, optionally, a block.

Always work within your own limits, starting with less intensity and fewer repetitions.

According to recent reports, lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the mat. Hug your right knee toward your chest and keep your left leg bent or straighten it on the mat. Hold your right shin with your hands or wrap a strap around it in Half Knees-to-Chest Pose (Ardha Apanasana). Press your shin against your hands or strap and, at the same time, pull your leg or the strap toward you. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other. Spend several breaths here, then switch sides.

Lie on your back and draw both knees toward your chest, keeping your hips on the mat. Grab hold of the outer edges of your feet or calves or hold the backs of your thighs. Keeping your knees bent, reach the soles of your feet toward the sky and widen your legs as you draw your knees toward your underarms in Happy Baby (Ananda Balasana). Push your feet or the backs of your thighs against your hands and, at the same time, pull down against your feet or thighs with your hands. Do this for several breaths, then release.

Sit tall with your legs straight in front of you. Bend your right knee and lean forward to grab hold of the outer edge of your right foot with your right hand or a strap. Lean back as you lift your right leg so your shin is about parallel to the mat in Archer Pose (Akarna Dhanurasana). Think of drawing your right foot back toward your right shoulder (similar to Happy Baby). Press your foot against your hand or the strap and, at the same time, pull your foot toward your shoulder. Stay here for a few breaths, then release and switch sides.

Sit tall with your legs straight in front of you. Bend your right leg and cross it over your left leg, stepping your right foot to the mat outside your left thigh. Bend your left leg and draw your left foot toward your right sitting bone as you lower your left knee toward the mat. Lean forward and grab your right foot with both hands or a strap. Lean back and lift your right leg in front of you, playing with how much you can comfortably straighten it while keeping your chest lifted and your back straight in a variation of Heron Pose (Krounchasana). Reach your heel away from you and, at the same time, pull your foot toward you with your hands or the strap. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other. Stay here for a few breaths, then release and switch sides.

Stand with your feet hip-distance apart or wider and fold forward into Standing Forward Bend, bending your knees as much as you need. Slide your hands, palms facing up, underneath your feet so your fingers are pointing toward your heels in Hand to Foot Pose (Pada Hastasana). Shift your weight into your feet and, at the same time, pull upward with your hands as if you are trying to lift your feet off the mat. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other. After several breaths here, step off your hands, and slowly rise to standing.

It has been revealed that stand facing the short edge of the mat and grab a strap. Step your left foot back and turn your toes out slightly. Lift the ball of your right foot so your toes point toward the sky. Loop the strap around the ball of your right foot, then stand upright. Slide your hands up the strap until your hands are alongside your hips and the strap is taut. Press into the strap with the ball of your foot and, at the same time, use your arms to keep the strap back against your hips for several breaths in this Pyramid Pose (Parsvottanasana) variation. You can intensify the stretch in your front leg by folding your chest forward with a flat back, adjusting your hands so that they remain alongside your hips and your strap stays taut. Continue to pull the strap toward you for a few breaths, then return to standing upright. Release the strap and switch sides.

In a recent development, stand facing the long edge of the mat and step your feet wide apart. Place your hands on your hips and lift your chest. Forward fold with a flat back, keeping your knees bent as much as you need, then hook your big toes with your index and middle fingers or place a strap underneath both feet in Wide-Legged Standing Forward Bend (Prasarita Padottanasana D). Press your feet down toward the mat and, at the same time, bend your elbows out to the sides as you pull the strap as if you were trying to lift it toward you. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other and away from your ears. After a few breaths here, release your grip, then slowly come up to standing.

According to recent reports, stand facing the short edge of the mat. Find a steady point straight in front of you at which to gaze. Press your left foot into the mat as you bend your right knee and lift your foot behind you toward your right sitting bone. Grab hold of your inner right foot with your right hand or wrap a strap around your right ankle and hold both ends in your right hand. Press your right foot behind you as you lean your chest forward into a slight backbend and reach your left arm forward in Dancer Pose (Natarajasana). Press your right foot toward the wall behind you and, at the same time, try to pull your foot forward with your right hand or strap. Stay here for several breaths, then switch sides.

Lie on your stomach with your legs straight, the tops of your feet against the mat, and your arms alongside you with your palms facing down. Lift your head and chest off the mat, keeping your gaze a few inches in front of you on the mat. Press your thighs against the mat as you bend your knees, draw your feet toward your sitting bones, and grasp your ankles with your hands or wrap a strap around them. Press your shins toward the wall behind you and, at the same time, try to pull your feet toward you with your hands or the strap as you lift yourself into Bow Pose (Dhanurasana). Stay here for several breaths, then release.

Come to your hands and knees. Draw your toes together and widen your knees. Sink your hips toward your heels as far as feels good, walk your hands as far out in front of you as you can, and lower your forehead to the mat or a block. Press your hands against the mat, imagining you’re sliding it toward you, lift your elbows off the mat, and draw your shoulder blades toward each other. Stay in this variation of Child’s Pose (Balasana) for several breaths, then slowly release the effort in your arms.

#22529. Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

📅 24 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1593 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Our Editors Ride-Tested Virginia Tech’s Top-Rated Road and Gravel Helmets—Including a $60 Pick That Punches Way Above Its Price

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times.
  • When shopping for latest road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a cyclist for over three decades, I’ve crashed many times. Unfortunately, I’ve also had a few concussions. Because of this, safety is important to me when I choose a new helmet. Over the last few seasons, I’ve tested dozens of great helmets, from budget picks under $50 to go-fast aero lids and lightweight models for over $500. Plus, I also test trail helmets, commuter lids, and everything in between.

When shopping for latest road and gravel helmets, cyclists often base their choices almost entirely on looks, price, and overall comfort. Depending on our riding goals and budget, we also balance weight, aerodynamics, and style. We want safety features, but many riders assume most helmets do a decent job of protecting our noggin—they’re all certified, right?

Helmet safety isn’t as straightforward as it may seem. Current Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standards—as well as more rigorous, voluntary requirements, such as those from ASTM—account for straight-line impacts and G-forces from a collision. These standards don’t address the rotational forces from a crash that contribute significantly to concussions and traumatic brain injuries. Plus, the CPSC’s standards took effect on March 10, 1999—advancements in technology, design, materials, and manufacturing over the last 27 years have changed bike helmets.

It has been revealed that so, what standards and certifications cover rotational forces? Currently, none. To better protect against rotational forces and reduce concussions, many brands incorporate Mips liners (and similar anti-rotational designs) into their helmets. Brands also test their helmets internally to their own, generally unpublished, criteria. The Virginia Tech helmet lab’s STAR score provides the best independent testing and ranking for helmets across most cycling disciplines.

Virginia Tech tests helmets for safety; it doesn’t evaluate fit, comfort, weight, price, or overall practicality. Bicycling’s test team collectively rides tens of thousands of miles each year on tarmac, gravel roads, singletrack, and commuting. That means we have a lot of time to ride-test lids—including more than half of Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR-rated road helmets.

For 15 years, Virginia Tech has tested helmets through a battery of 24 impact tests that analyse safety performance and assign an overall STAR (Summation of Tests for the Analysis of Risk) score.

In a recent development, “The overall score estimates the number of concussions the average person would see if they experienced identical impacts at rates matching their weightings while cycling,” claims Virginia Tech’s lab. The lower the STAR score, the better a helmet performed in testing.

Then, to each helmet it tests, Virginia Tech awards an overall STAR rating (one through five); helmets with four- and five-STARs are “recommended.” The lab does not recommend helmets scoring three STARs or fewer.

According to recent reports, virginia Tech has tested and published results on more than 300 bicycle helmets. To date, the lab has awarded 56 helmets its coveted 5-STAR rating, and another 104 received 4 STARs. To make researching and choosing a new helmet easier, it also sorts the helmets it tests into mountain, road, urban, multi-sport, full-face, and E-bike categories. Of the 5-STAR helmets, 21 of them are road lids.

Editor’s Note: These helmets are the top 5-rated road bike helmets in Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet rankings as of November 9, 2026. The Virginia Tech helmet lab regularly tests helmets and updates the overall rankings; the top 5 can change at any time. Please consult Virginia Tech’s bicycle helmet ranking list for up-to-date rankings.

“Who is Pikio?” and “What is a Si Oblik?” Those were the questions our editors all asked when we saw this helmet rocket to the top of Virginia Tech’s STAR ratings. The Pikio isn’t only the top-rated road helmet; it’s also Virginia Tech’s best-performing helmet, period. It beats the others by a considerable margin, logging an unbelievably low 4.61 STAR score. For context, the difference between the Pikio and the second-place overall Canyon Deflectr RLS mountain bike helmet is 2.21 points; that’s the same gap between the 2nd and 28th positions in current rankings.

All of that safety comes at a relatively steep $379 cost. While the Si Oblik’s price aligns with other range-topping helmets from Giro, POC, Specialized, and MET, Pikio’s looks and finish feel comparable to mid-tier models from more well-known brands. For example, Pikio’s color options are somewhat conservative choices, and the rear strap anchor point is through-shell.

Industry observers note that the Si Oblik fits well and has a broad range of adjustment for my medium-sized head. The rear adjusts up and down (to account for head shape and hairstyles) and features a dial to microadjust fit. The straps, however, are not as cleanly executed as expected for the price, especially compared to POC or Specialized, and I found them slightly tedious to adjust. On road and gravel rides, the Si Oblik’s airflow doesn’t feel bad, but I didn’t test this lid in peak summer heat. And while the Pikio weighs about the same as Giro and MET helmets in this test, it feels physically bigger, though not as mushroomy as the POC Cytal.

For a new brand, Pikio Labs made a solid first effort. Unlike its competitors, Pikio doesn’t have decades of trial and error or a flashy WorldTour team. Hopefully, as the manufacturer grows, it can dial in details, sharpen pricing, and spice up the aesthetic, because the Si Oblik already sets a very high bar for safety.

According to recent reports, the POC Cytal’s unique shape and bold look make it easy to spot in a peloton. Another reason the Cytal stands out is due to its overall size—it’s a physically big lid. But despite its dimensions and slightly heavy weight, it doesn’t feel that large on your head while riding and ventilates surprisingly well.

In a recent development, the Cytal’s great ventilation comes from its massive vents and internal air channels that funnel air directly over your forehead while riding. I found out how well it vents while riding over the summer in France during “la canicule” (the heatwave). I could still feel the Cytal pushing air in 100-degree temps, even if it was roasting hot.

Sources indicate that in our recent review of P2R’s $100 aero-helmet, ride tester Tom Messina remarked it “has no business being this good.” And with its lower price and STAR score, we say the same thing about P2R’s $60 A20 Mips. With its excellent safety rating, great adjustability, and budget-friendly price, the A20 Mips outperforms many helmets that cost three, four, or even five times its price.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road.

The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it on said it was a little snug near their temples.

Given the Trenta 3K Carbon’s pedigree, it’s hard not to name it “Best for Racing.” UAE Team Emirates’ official sponsor is MET, and the Trenta is one of the helmets it supplies to the squad—including Tour de France champion Tadej Pogačar and World Champion Brandon McNulty. While UAE riders often race the Italian brand’s Manta aero helmet, they sometimes pick the lightweight, well-ventilated Trenta 3K Carbon for climbing stages and training.

Unlike some modern helmets with similarly strong protection, the Trenta feels light and racey on your head, and almost disappears when you’re riding. The straps offer good adjustability, and the Mips Air Node liner protects without feeling bulky. However, the Trenta’s biggest drawback is its price tag. At over $500, this is an expensive piece of kit.

In a recent development, ranked 14th overall and 5th in road helmets, Giro’s Aries Spherical stands out in our testing for its overall comfort, adjustability, low weight, and great looks. While its STAR score is much higher than the first-place Pikio, the Aries is a very safe helmet and received Virginia Tech’s 5-STAR rating. Having crashed on the road while wearing an Aries Spherical, I also know this helmet works.

Of the approximately one dozen road and gravel helmets in my rotation at any given time, I reach for the Aries Spherical most often. The Aries fits my head perfectly, and the Roc Loc dial system offers plenty of adjustability for hair length or if I’m wearing a cap underneath in rain or cold weather. Giro makes the Aries in a wide range of colors and graphics to fit almost any rider’s personality or fashion.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Fresh England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour.
  • The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent.
  • In a recent development, 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Wagner Araujo/World Triathlon).

In a recent development, the postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

In a recent development, 2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Recent findings suggest that isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would quickly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Recent findings suggest that halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

By halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

In a recent development, that momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”.

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

Industry observers note that in the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of new world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

Sources indicate that latest Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other major name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

Industry observers note that it started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

According to recent reports, perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and organization. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the significant question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Sources indicate that onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde promptly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

Recent findings suggest that the front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He quickly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

In a recent development, it was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”.

Recent findings suggest that wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

#22524. 5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

5 Wellness Trends We’d Like to See Go Away

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that let’s talk about wellness trends.
  • It has been revealed that being a person is not always easy.
  • Industry observers note that routines that can support your physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” Many of these approaches include habits that support your life and health—those that truly make you feel good.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that let’s talk about wellness trends. More specifically, let’s talk about our collective penchant for “optimizing” the human experience.

It has been revealed that being a person is not always easy. We’re all in bodies that are designed to decay, with minds that tend to run amok and emotions that can seem like that have brains of their own. It’s only natural to try to control what we can—and self-care provides what can seem like an ideal platform for the pursuit.

Industry observers note that routines that can support your physical, emotional, and mental well-being fall under the ever-growing umbrella of “wellness.” Many of these approaches include habits that support your life and health—those that truly make you feel good. Unfortunately, many wellness trends begin in a beneficial place and spiral out of control from there.

A growing corner of self-care tends to be overly focused on tracking, streamlining, and pushing extremes. Any wellness trends that make you feel inadequate or anxious (like the examples listed below), are the ones we’d love to fade into the background.

Take what, if anything, really works for you from the below trends and then notice when it’s time to let it go.

It has been revealed that the concept of “sleepmaxxing,” or maximizing the quality of your sleep, began swirling around social media a couple of years ago. Sleeping better is a trend we can get behind—but you don’t need expensive gadgets or high levels of anxiety to do it. More importantly, putting too much focus on your sleep habits has the potential to backfire, transforming a restful part of your day into a stressful one.

Recent findings suggest that good sleep is essential. Nicole Moshfegh, MD, clinical psychologist and author of The Book of Sleep, notes that proper (or inadequate) rest can affect your physical health and cognitive function, not to mention your mood. Sleep is meant to be restful. Relaxing. Restorative.

It has been revealed that your sleep routine should not be causing you additional stress. If habits like evening restorative yoga, breathwork, or less blue light after dark improve your sleep quality, maxx on! But should you find yourself agonizing over a sleep score or lying awake calculating how many minutes of rest you’re losing—both examples of orthosomnia—know that you’ve lost the plot.

Dunking your body into cold water might sound refreshing—and for some of the population, it is! Cold plunging is a Nordic tradition that boosts mental clarity and resilience (again, you are willingly submerging yourself in cold water) and is thought to reduce post-workout muscle stiffness, fatigue, and more.

Still, you may want to pause before adopting the cold plunge as your new cure-all. One study suggests that using cold baths for muscle recovery may be more of a placebo effect than anything else, as parsed by writer Alex Hutchinson. And for those in female bodies, further research has shown that over time, exposure to cold water can adversely effect the reproductive system, and there is no proven boon to female muscle recovery.

Between phone apps, smart watches, and bluetooth-connected rings, it’s never been easier to know exactly what’s going on in your body, at least on a biological level.

In a recent development, certain smart gadgets, like the Pulse Mindfulness Ring, can act as a little buddy, helping you breathe deeply, commit to daily meditation, and focus. And when used correctly, the Oura Ring can also be a mindful companion.

Sources indicate that the glitch isn’t the tracking devices themselves, but how they’re being used. Just as putting too much stock in sleep scores can be considered an obsessive condition (again, orthosomnia), too much preoccupation with the information provided by wearable devices is proven to negatively impact psychological well-being. For some—including those with eating or health disorders—this sort of constant tracking can serve as a trigger, increasing rigidity and anxiety around otherwise healthy habits.

In short, try taking your smart accessories off sometimes, just to see how you feel.

We live in a world where the breaking news about what’s going on in our minds and bodies—and, usually, what we’re lacking—is practically non-stop. And usually, there’s a supplement for that. According to one report, the global supplement market is projected to be worth $300 billion by 2028. So…ya.

Industry observers note that supplementing becomes an problem when you’re adding to your stack before looking to your diet and other habits. Studies have shown that supplements and weight loss pills offer a perceived sense of invulnerability, ironically leading to poorer choices in nutrition and fitness habits.

In a recent development, another more obvious issue is supplements offered with no scientific evidence to back up purported benefits. Fast-moving digital culture and lack of oversight means that brands can pretty much say whatever they want to, which is a good thing to remember before putting anything in your body.

If your supplements are thoughtfully chosen and supplementing an existing healthy lifestyle, you’re probably on the positive side of this trend.

Industry observers note that the internet can make your life feel like a reality show. And if you make your living as an influencer, maybe it sort of is. But even with audience perception, brand deals, and showmanship at stake, your health and wellness routine can and should make you feel good.

At its core, self-care is for you. If sharing your journey feels beneficial for you and for them, go ahead. But when your wellness practices become more about the performance of tending to yourself and less about actually doing things that bring you peace and healing, you may want to reconsider your approach.

In a recent development, you might know New Balance as the preeminent source of dad shoes—those chunky, overlay-clad sneakers ubiquitous among lawn-mowing, beer-drinking guys of a certain age. Yes, New Balance still makes these kicks (and they’re actually back in style), but that’s just a small sliver of this tech giant’s story.

Industry observers note that new Balance is a highly respected brand with a long history: The company was founded in 1906 in Boston and originally sold arch supports. Among runners, New Balance has a reputation for creating reliable training shoes with a strong emphasis on comfort. The Ellipse, which earned a 2026 Shoe Award, is a great example: It’s a cushioned, stable, bouncy trainer that works well for a wide swath of runners.

In recent years, the brand has broadened its lineup beyond trusty workhorse shoes with models like the SuperComp Elite, a carbon-plated speed shoe designed for racing. Today, New Balance is on the cutting edge—no lawn mower required.

According to recent reports, this guide highlights the top pairs in the Latest Balance stable. The brand makes something for everyone, and there are well-regarded models here to suit all kinds of runners, including supportive trainers, max-cushion sneakers, racing shoes, and even trail shoes. Read on to learn more about the key tech NB uses in its shoes and dive into our favorite pairs below.

Shopping for a neutral trainer → Upcoming Balance Fresh Foam X 880v15 (Men’s/Women’s)On a budget → New Balance Fresh Foam 680v9 (Men’s/Women’s)Looking for a bargain → New Balance Ellipse (Men’s/Women’s)Hooked on carbon → New Balance SuperComp Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)In need of a plush ride → New Balance Fresh Foam X 1080v15 (Men’s/Women’s)Sticking to the trails → New Balance Fresh Foam X Hierro v9 (Men’s/Women’s)Running intervals and fartleks → New Balance FuelCell Rebel v5 (Men’s/Women’s)Racing → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)Rolling your foot inward (overpronating) → New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v15 (Men’s/Women’s).

Recent findings suggest that to write this guide, I talked with a Latest Balance brand rep and reviewed the tech giant’s lineup to learn more about its latest models and shoe tech. I chose the shoes you see below, making sure to include models that showcase the best New Balance tech and design approaches as well as shoes for different running disciplines.

The 880 is one of Upcoming Balance’s core training shoes, and the v15 is a real standout: RW testers called it “one shoe that can do it all,” and it earned a 2025 Shoe Award thanks to its versatility and stable ride.

In a recent development, the 880 is a neutral trainer that features an EVA-based Fresh Foam X midsole. New Balance bumped the stack height to more than 40 mm for v15, giving this shoe even more cushioning (at the cost of increased weight). But as Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate notes in his review, the shoe doesn’t feel pillowy soft. Instead, it’s surprisingly stable: The thick midsole takes the sting out of impacts and feels planted underfoot, and combined with the 880’s snug upper, the shoe serves up a comfortable, predictable ride that’s great for everyday training.

In a recent development, the 880 is classic Newly introduced Balance: a trusty workhorse that’ll keep your feet happy through neighborhood jogs and long runs alike (one tester even liked it for speed workouts). If reliability and comfort are your top priorities for running shoes, you can’t go wrong with this model.

It’s surprisingly durable for accruing miles, and you won’t feel like you’re slogging because it’s anything but beefy.

The shoe has an accommodating fit in the midfoot area, though some commented the toebox feels slightly narrow. You can go up a size—or up a width. The 680v9 comes in wide (men’s, women’s) and extra wide (men’s).

Upcoming Balance Fresh Foam 680v9 Review.

The Ellipse, included in our 2026 Shoe Awards, is the shoe version of a run friend. Meant to encapsulate the feeling of going on a group run, Upcoming Balance’s newest shoe has plush, supportive foam that makes your runs feel easier and bouncier.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

We get it—you want to run in your carbon-plated, super foam shoes every day. Thing is, with the exception of a few test runs, you should save your super shoes for race day so they stay fresh. Here’s where the SC Rebel comes in. New Balance created a carbon-plated shoe specifically for training. It’s intended to make your runs feel easier as you reap the propulsion from the carbon plate and TPEE-based Infinion foam.

Furrer took the SC Rebel out on a long run over road and trail, and found the shoe’s traction reliable on both surfaces. “The shoe has a wider platform that helps with stability; it has more support than your standard super shoe,” she mentioned. “I was impressed with the snap and slightly spongy but not aggressive rebound. I trusted the shoe over loose dirt and pavement pocked with potholes.”.

According to recent reports, the plush 1080, which we also included in our 2026 Shoe Awards, gets a major patch in its latest iteration. The team swapped the EVA-based Fresh Foam midsole for Infinion. Composed of supercritical TPEE and TPU-based, Infinion is more durable and delivers a bouncier ride. It has been revealed that “The Infinion Foam tends to hit that balance I look for in a daily trainer—it has some pop in the cushioning without being too soft,” stated tester and Director of Content Operations Brian Dalek. “And it lasts a long time. Recent findings suggest that the Hierro v9 features a dual-density Fresh Foam X midsole: a soft top layer cushions impacts and creates a plush underfoot feel, and a firmer lower layer stabilizes the shoe and keeps sharp debris from poking up into your feet. The mesh upper is designed to breathe well, and overlays keep your feet protected from scrapes against rocks and brush. RW testers gave the Hierro high marks overall, and they especially loved its cushy Fresh Foam X midsole: “For comfort over distance, it’s one of the best I’ve tried,” one tester stated.

According to recent reports, upcoming Balance has been steadily tweaking the Rebel over the past couple iterations, and the latest edition offers significantly increased cushioning while still maintaining a feathery weight. This is a great shoe for speed training, although it serves up a comfy overall feel that works well at slower speeds, too.

In a recent development, like the v4, the Rebel v5 features a blend of PEBA and EVA foams in its FuelCell midsole. The main difference? Despite the shoe’s firmer platform, O’Connor described the ride as “super comfortable the entire run.”.

The Rebel lacks the carbon-fiber plate found in its race-oriented sibling, the SuperComp Elite, so it can’t quite achieve super shoe levels of bounciness from its midsole. Even so, runners say it feels peppy, and its more streamlined sole design makes it very comfortable at a wide range of paces.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

According to recent reports, newly introduced Balance seems to revamp its super shoes every year, with no two models looking—or riding—alike. And we’re here for that ride. In lieu of FuelCell, the brand switched in a lighter and bouncier version of Infinion, the new foam introduced in the max-cushioned 1080v15. It’s a move we’re seeing lots of brands participate in, such as Saucony and Asics, swapping PEBA for A-TPU, or in this case, TPEE.

This makes the SuperComp Elite v6 even lighter than its predecessor (although, all things considered, the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 was a chonk). To shave off even more weight, the upper is replaced with translucent mesh, which gives the shoe a track flat vibe.

The shoe isn’t as aggressive as some of its competitors, and a couple testers found the cushioning firm. But the accommodating fit in the midfoot area provided comfort over long miles when testers’ feet began to swell. The plush cushioning in the heel was also a favorite feature, especially for heel strikers.

Industry observers note that “Very comfy for long miles,” said shoe tester Josh Davis. “You can definitely wear these in a marathon and count on the comfort to last.”.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

Industry observers note that now on its 15th iteration, the 860 is a trusted workhorse trainer that offers a supportive feel and good cushioning for routine training miles. The latest version has the 14’s newly introduced last and rocker shape for smooth strides; it also includes the previous iteration’s Stability Plane, a thin, stiff EVA-based midsole plate that supports the foot.

The 860 is built with a relatively wide full-contact sole, which gives it some inherent stability. The midsole features two flavors of Fresh Foam X plus the embedded Stability Plane. There’s a denser, harder layer of foam at the bottom, and it works in concert with the rigid Stability Plane to resist overpronation and support the foot. The top layer of the midsole is a softer version of Fresh Foam X that absorbs impact forces for a plush feel.

With its somewhat heavy build and comfort-oriented midsole design, the 860 isn’t the smartest choice for tempo runs, but testers loved it for general training, and it’s a great pick for those who need some extra support under their feet.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Midsole foams are the main technology that differentiates New Balance shoes. Like other shoe brands, New Balance has entered the foam wars by engineering its own proprietary cushioning foams. There are two key ones to know: Fresh Foam and FuelCell.

The latest version of Fresh Foam is Fresh Foam X, and it’s used in the brand’s workhorse training shoes, including stalwart models like the 880, 1080, and 860. This is an EVA-based foam that’s formulated for softness, and it gives these shoes a well-padded feel underfoot. Fresh Foam X serves up a comfortable ride that’s ideal for casual running and day-to-day training.

Industry observers note that fuelCell is used in Latest Balance’s speed-oriented models, like the Rebel and SuperComp Elite, and it’s optimized for energy return and responsiveness. New Balance tweaks the exact formula of this foam depending on the shoe and its intended use.

The training-oriented Rebel has a FuelCell midsole made from a blend of EVA and polyether block amide (PEBA)—a lightweight, soft, and very springy material that’s used in many brands’ speed shoes. This blend gives the Rebel a good balance of shock absorption and bounce.

Sources indicate that the race-focused SuperComp Elite, however, has a FuelCell midsole made entirely from PEBA, which saves weight while still allowing for a very thick layer of cushioning. It’s paired with a carbon-fiber plate that stabilizes your foot as you run and helps you get maximum squish—and propulsive energy return—from the hefty slice of foam. The result is a bouncy, propulsive ride that helps you push the pace, and it’s a great choice for race day.

According to recent reports, introduced with the 1080v15, Infinion foam is lighter and bouncier than the brand’s Fresh Foam X. New Balance has also tweaked Infinion for its racing collection of shoes. The TPEE-based foam in the SuperComp Elite v6 and SC Rebel delivers higher rebound, working with the rocker profile to encourage fast turnover, and the Energy Arc carbon plate, which helps stabilize the foam and provides propulsion.

For decades, Newly introduced Balance has used a number system to name its shoes—you’re probably familiar with classic models like the 990. The number system encompasses a broad range of shoes, including many casual pairs not designed for running. The numbered models intended for running (like the 1080) are training shoes that have been a part of the New Balance lineup for years.

By breaking up the model number, you can decipher the shoe’s intended use. Start at the end: The last two digits denote the model’s level of support. Shoes with names ending in 80 are neutral shoes, while shoes ending in 60 are stability shoes designed to counter overpronation. Shoes that end in 40, like the 1540, are old-school motion-control shoes with maximum support to bolster the foot.

Recent findings suggest that higher model numbers generally indicate the shoe has more midsole tech and more cushioning. The 1080, for example, is built with top-tier Fresh Foam X cushioning and has more overall padding than the 680, which uses an older version of Fresh Foam.

An crucial caveat: Many New Balance running shoes have unique names (like the Hierro and Rebel) and do not follow this number system at all.

What type of races should I choose the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer and SuperComp Elite for?

Recent findings suggest that the Pacer is lighter and leaner than the Elite, making it a better choice for shorter, faster races like a 5K, 10K, or even a half marathon. The Elite has more midsole cushioning (its heel stack is 5mm taller than the Pacer), so it’s better suited for longer efforts, like a marathon, where the added cushioning can help reduce foot fatigue.

What are good budget shoes from Upcoming Balance if I don’t want to spend over $140?

Besides the 680v9 on this list, the Kaiha Road v2 is a solid pick for budget-conscious runners. You’ll get a well-padded ride that’ll feel comfortable for both running and walking. The Ellipse is also worth considering. Even though it’s priced at $150, it’s our best value shoe because of its incredible comfort and responsive bounce. Premium materials guarantee longer shelf life, so you truly get your money’s worth.

Michael is a freelance writer with years of experience covering gear and the outdoors for Runner's World and other publications; when he's not writing, he's usually biking, hiking, and running in the mountains around Los Angeles, where he lives.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Industry observers note that fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Cloudsurfer 3 is a real step forward for On, even though it’s most definitely a daily trainer built with max cushioning for easy miles.
  • Right now, it’s only available in-store and at selected retailers, but it releases nationwide February 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Cloudsurfer 3 is a real step forward for On, even though it’s most definitely a daily trainer built with max cushioning for easy miles. It doesn’t have the pop of the brand’s bouncier shoes, and I don’t think it’s trying to. What it has in abundance is a steady, firm-soft (not a contradiction) cushion that holds up over long, easy miles, plus a fit that works beautifully for my feet.

Right now, it’s only available in-store and at selected retailers, but it releases nationwide February 2027.

The headline is Surreal, On’s first supercritical midsole foam, which is EVA-based and sits inside a redesigned CloudTec Phase structure. Supercritical processing infuses the foam with gas under high pressure and temperature, then lets it expand in an autoclave—a machine that uses steam to superheat the environment. That’s the same basic-ish idea behind the “super foams” that have taken over daily trainers, but On had never made it work with its hollow Clouds.

According to recent reports, scott Maguire, president and COO of On, explained why in an interview with Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “We’ve only ever been able to do CloudTec in EVA in the past,” he mentioned. “We’ve never been able to do it in a supercritical processing.”.

Industry observers note that the trouble was scale. “Putting Clouds in that, it becomes super small and it has to become very substantial,” Maguire said. Predicting where each Cloud will form, how far apart they sit, and how they interact “has been impossible for us to do for years.”.

On’s own numbers put Surreal at roughly 15 percent softer, 15 percent lighter, and 23.3 percent more responsive than Helion, the foam that came before Surreal. The redesigned CloudTec Phase geometry is credited with 15.5 percent deeper compression and a 9.9 percent cut in peak braking force. Those figures come from finite element analysis simulations at On Labs Zurich, so they are modeled results, not data from everyday runners; a grain of salt should be well-applied. What I felt in the ride was a foam that’s soft but has a firm backbone, kind of like a good honeycomb-cushion feeling.

Here’s where my opinion comes in. The new foam is an improvement, but the return doesn’t have quite the oomph of other shoes in On’s lineup. If you’re hoping for a springy kickoff, look elsewhere.

What I love is the character of the cushion. It’s firm-softness—if that’s a thing—which I declare it is. Over long miles, it never felt like it compacted, and it never gave so much that it slowed me down. Since I run more miles than speed, that’s my best case.

In a recent development, dengate, who has been tough on On’s hole-based tech in the past because slabs of modern foam were beating it, came around: The Cloudsurfer 3 “really does feel like a substantial improvement in comfort and ride for a daily training shoe.” Gear Editor Amanda Furrer, who admits she found past On trainers kind of blah, rated this one near-perfect. As a cushioned trainer, she remarked she’d have to quote me, saying: “it’s aces.”.

On gets fit so right. From its super shoes to its ultra trail runners like the Cloudultra Pro, they’re somehow both forgiving and secure, with a heel-lock eyelet placement that’s my personal favorite bit of the brand. (That, and the Zendaya commercials. I love her.).

Recent findings suggest that I have high arches and a correspondingly high instep, and this shoe suits both. There was no rubbing and no hot spots, and I never felt the need to loosen my laces at the midfoot. The warp-knit upper is plush through the collar and tongue and secure without clamping or getting that weird bunching pleat thing that I loathe.

In a recent development, furrer saw the same thing from the wide-foot side. For runners with wide feet and high insteps, she states, the “Cloudsurfer is fitted and not tight, but also secure.”.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a speedwork shoe. If you want a rocket for tempo days, keep looking. It’s also on the heavier side, which is the trade-off for all that stack.

But as an everyday trainer for long, easy miles, it’s excellent. The foam is better, the fit is better, and the ride stays consistent from the first mile to the last. For high-arched runners especially, I’d put it near the top of the try-on list.

#22517. As a Back-of-the-Pack Runner, I Always Struggled to Run at Different Paces—Until I Tried This Approach

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (770 w)
📖 Baca

As a Back-of-the-Pack Runner, I Always Struggled to Run at Different Paces—Until I Tried This Approach

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app.
  • Disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds.
  • According to recent reports, fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was a hot summer afternoon on Cold Soil Road, and I had just finished the “First Speed Run,” a guided run in the Nike Run Club app. It included eight one-minute inter­vals interspersed with one minute of recovery. The virtual coach of that run prescribed different speeds, including a mile pace which was “fast,” a 10K pace which was “faster, but slower than a mile pace,” and the slowest of the three, a marathon pace. No matter how much I tried, I couldn’t run at different paces. Over the course of my various flirtations, romances, and relationships with running, I’d always seemed to move at only two speeds: run and walk.

Disappointed and discouraged, I checked to see the name of the next guided run, hoping it wouldn’t force me to struggle, yet again, with unrealistic speeds. The name? “Find Your Pace.” Excited about this fortuitous opportunity, I pressed download and started this short workout even though I had just struggled through the previous one.

According to recent reports, fortunately, Coach Cory, who led this particular guided run, never once asked me to check my Fitbit for metrics and pace. Instead, he only referred to the Rate of Perceived Exertion, a metric that has been around for decades, but that I had, to be honest, ignored for all of that time. RPE is a purely subjective scale from 1 to 10. Typically, 1 refers to an effort level similar to sitting on your couch (i.e., no effort at all), and running at a 3 is a warmup effort. On the other end of the spectrum is 10, an all-out sprint, a pace you can’t sustain for more than half a minute.

Coach Cory explained that my effort level, or exertion, correlated to a variety of distances. For example, I should strive to run a 10K at an RPE of 6, a 5K at 7, and one mile at 9.

He also suggested that runners connect words to different effort levels—for example, the word “strong” when running at the RPE of 6. Honestly, though? At 6, I thought, This is hard, and at 7, I can’t do this. By the time I reached 9, I thought, I have to stop. Coach Cory, on the other hand, suggested I use the word “epic” to describe my fastest pace. He’s clearly an optimist.

Recent findings suggest that these were very short intervals, so my breathing and heart rate didn’t rise much. But the difference I felt between this run and my previous runs was notable: I was pushing myself in a way I had never done before. I followed Coach Cory’s instructions back and forth on the same block, and not once did I look at my Fitbit or the app to see how fast I was going, which is what I was instructed to do during my previous runs. The whole exercise was over in 10 minutes. You may be thinking, Well, okay, but how fast were you? Did you actually run at different paces?

It has been revealed that turns out, yes, I did. Even more shocking, I had truly picked up speed during these intervals. My mile pace was 9:21, my 5K was 10:30, and my 10K was 10:54. Faster than I’ve ever run during a training run or race. During that one short workout, I realized I could create different paces based on my effort rather than trying to “find” different paces for each race distance.

It has been revealed that I know that might seem like semantics, but the difference is meaningful. “Finding” something isn’t in your control, but “creating” is. When a training initiative listed different goal paces, I couldn’t seem to reach them, but when I ran based on my RPE, I was able to distinguish between different efforts, and those effort levels translated to mile, 5K, and 10K paces.

This run was memorable. It gave me a boost to not give up on myself or my training. It let me know what was possible if I kept training. Now when a race plan instructs me to run at a 5K or 10K pace, I don’t worry about the speed metrics. Instead, I focus on my effort. Turns out I can create paces even if I can’t find them.

How Restorative Yoga Can Help Lessen the Effects of Stress

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
