📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that most runners are familiar with the massive muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still important—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.

A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.

When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, notes Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.

If this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew indicates. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.

There are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In particular, when the psoas (a big, rope-like hip flexor muscle that runs from your lower back to the front of your hip) is shortened, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, meaning your pelvis is tipped forward, arching your lower back. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.

Industry observers note that another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

Yet another cause of an irritated QL is upper-back stiffness. Restrictions in the upper part of the spine can shift more workload onto the QL, Haas explains. So can issues in your shoulders, hips, and mid-back. If these areas aren’t moving like they should due to pain or injury, your QL may receive added stress, Haas indicates.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that in some cases, your QL may hurt because it’s taking on a bunch of extra stress it’s not meant to, but the muscle itself probably isn’t tight. “It’s more like your QL is just irritated because everything has been collapsing around it and loading it,” Haas notes. “It’s overworked and underappreciated.”.

Recent findings suggest that A tight-feeling QL is worth addressing because it can lead to a few not-so-great problems if left unchecked. A major one? Compromised running mechanics.

A tight QL, as mentioned, can shorten your hip flexors and pull your pelvis into an anterior tilt, which will reduce your knee lift as you stride, Agnew states. As a result, “you’re not going to be able to generate as much force moving forward, and you’ll have more of an arched-back position when you run,” he explains. In many cases, this can deliver a double whammy of reduced performance and increased back pain, he says.

According to recent reports, on top of that, a tight QL can also hinder your breathing. As mentioned above, one of the QL’s jobs is to help you inhale, so when this muscle is tight, you may not be able to breathe as deeply or easily, Agnew says.

According to recent reports, plagued by what you think may be an irritated QL? Try Agnew’s three-step at-home series to help reduce your discomfort.

According to recent reports, perform this sequence as often as every day if you’re in significant discomfort that’s limiting your ability to run. In the case of minor pain, incorporate this series two to three times per week. On the days you run, perform the myofascial release, pelvic tilts, and hip hikes before you lace up, then tackle the other components afterward.

This can help turn down the pain response in a barking QL by desensitizing soft tissue, Agnew explains.

How to Perform Myofascial Release.

In a recent development, the pelvic tilts help you learn how to coordinate and control pelvic motion so you can maintain proper mechanics while running, and the hip hikes help activate your QL. The kettlebell side bend increases blood flow to the muscle, which can aid in healing. Finally, the suitcase carry increases strength, stability, and engagement of the muscle, which can ensure it functions properly during a run.

Lengthen your QL—as well as tight hip flexors—with this two-for-one half-kneeling lunge stretch.

According to recent reports, do these moves daily or several times per day to mobilize your lower back. Perform them before or after a run. Important caveat: If your QL hurts more after stretching—or if your QL pain returns soon after stretching—then stretches are likely not the solution and you should stop doing them, Haas explains.

Dynamic QL Mobility + Hip 90/90.

According to recent reports, to start, do one set of these moves daily to help your body learn the neuromuscular patterns. (The caveat: If you feel sore, then skip a day.) After about six weeks, do these moves two to three times per week as part of your regular strength-training routine.

Industry observers note that this exercise targets the glutes and works on pelvic control in a movement pattern that’s similar to running. Think of it as an opportunity to train proper glute use in your running form, which will help unload any strain on your QL caused by weak glutes.

Industry observers note that this exercise can improve core stability and strengthen the glutes, resulting in improved running mechanics and less stress on your QL. You’ll need a long, looped resistance band.

In a recent development, sometimes, despite your best at-home efforts to treat an irritated QL, it’s still best to get checked out by a physical therapist. Haas recommends booking a PT appointment if you try the above stretches and strength moves and don’t see improvements after about two weeks.

Agnew suggests getting evaluated by a PT if you’re in so much pain that it’s inhibiting your running. In this case, getting seen sooner can help mitigate pain before further issues arise, Agnew explains.

Here’s What to Know About the Nike Vaporfly 5

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a upcoming method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear.
  • The substantial highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a upcoming method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”.

The substantial highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a upcoming, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”.

It has been revealed that I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

Remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

According to recent reports, world Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this latest plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the massive carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

With these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool new innovations revealed, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more swiftly, which can be customized for various applications.

It has been revealed that I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

In a recent development, nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

Sources indicate that these new units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Industry observers note that jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

#22491. This is What Happens When You Slow Down Long Enough to Be Curious

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1518 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogajournal ↗ Open Full Page

This is What Happens When You Slow Down Long Enough to Be Curious

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s one thing to know you need to slow things down in your everyday experience of life—to slow your thoughts, your breath, your attention, your scrolling, even your assumptions.
  • Neuroscientists tell us that life changes at the end of our comfort zone.
  • However, we often decide in advance how things will go, or assume we know how another person is feeling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s one thing to know you need to slow things down in your everyday experience of life—to slow your thoughts, your breath, your attention, your scrolling, even your assumptions. It’s an entirely different thing to know how to slow down. Longtime mindfulness teacher, yoga therapist, and author Jillian Pransky addresses that disconnect in her recent book, The Power of the Pause: 90 Seconds to Calm, Reset, and Reconnect. In its pages, she explains exactly how pausing can alchemize everyday interactions in ways you’ve probably never considered. The following excerpt from the “Pausing in Our Discomfort Zone” chapter shows how slowing down can help you experience a more nuanced understanding of not only yourself but those who approach the world from a different perspective than you—and why that can benefit everyone. —Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ.

Neuroscientists tell us that life changes at the end of our comfort zone. The ability to build new neural pathways is called neuroplasticity, and it happens not only from repeating “new” behaviors, but also when we reach beyond what we know and explore new territories. Whether learning a new skill or facing a fear, your brain actively creates new neural connections, enhancing cognitive abilities, memory, and overall brain health.

However, we often decide in advance how things will go, or assume we know how another person is feeling. These assumptions can keep us stuck in patterns of behaviors or relationship dynamics that simply strengthen our resistance to change. When we remind ourselves that we have space to change, we often begin to see that there might be more going on than we think. We can open up to paradox, contradiction, and complexity in ways we were not able to before.

We may realize that no way is the only way. That we don’t need to make anything one way. And that things don’t always have to be precisely the way we want them.

It has been revealed that pausing helps us create support and safety for ourselves, giving us the confidence and courage to go beyond our comfort zone. Gradually titrating, step-by-step, into new territory allows our brain to integrate these changes, leading to our personal growth and evolution.

It has been revealed that dr. Gail Parker, psychologist, international presenter, and author of the self-care book Restorative Yoga for Ethnic and Race-Based Stress and Trauma, emphasizes that curiosity is essential for opening space in our conversations for connection, particularly among disparate groups of people.

She says, “You can make someone else feel safe when you are curious rather than judgmental, assuming, or indifferent. In the face of listening to others, especially those we don’t know so well or those from another culture, it’s notable to remember that we can’t know everything about others or every culture, but what we can do is be curious about others.”.

According to recent reports, listening includes being aware of ourselves and how we feel while conversing with another. In this way, we can learn to notice our own expectations and emotions, stay curious about ourselves, and hold space for ourselves and the other person. Dr. Parker suggests Pausing to check in with ourselves during conversations, with questions like:.

Sources indicate that • Am I truly listening? • Am I making assumptions? • Do I have expectations? • What am I feeling?

If we can stay aware of ourselves and curious about our feelings, we won’t get stuck in what we are feeling. “A key to remember is that if we can notice when we are in the stress response, we are not stuck in it,” she indicates.

Hala Khouri, author of several books, co-editor of Practicing Liberation: Transformative Strategies for Collective Healing and Systems Change, and co-founder of the social activism organization Off the Mat, Into the World, also emphasizes curiosity as an essential cornerstone for connection in difficult conversations.

Khouri, who is also a therapist, yoga teacher, and somatic experience practitioner, contends that curiosity is not only a portal for going deeper into our conversations, but is also the key to helping us know when it is time to leave a conversation—or not have one at all.

“When we are in conversation with another, I think it is crucial to ask ourselves, can I be curious right now? If we can’t get curious, that might be a good indicator that we need a break or need to remove ourselves from the conversation or situation, if that is an option,” she states.

The main point is that we need to stay connected to ourselves so we can sense our internal state. True listening requires curiosity. If we can’t be curious, that’s essential information for us. And, when we are highly activated in the stress response, we cannot simultaneously be curious. That part of our brain is not accessible when we are in fight-or-flight mode.

Whenever you notice you can’t be curious, take a moment to Pause and care for yourself until you can get your curiosity back.

If we could consciously choose to enter conversations with the intention to Listen—to be curious—to understand the other person’s experience a little bit better, maybe even put ourselves in their shoes, we might be able to learn from people in our lives whose world views are different from ours or even opposed to ours.

It can be helpful to remember that leading with curiosity rather than certainty doesn’t automatically mean that someone else is right. Or that we are wrong. But it opens a space in which we might connect rather than shut down to each other. The goal is not necessarily to reach agreement with others, but to understand each other. For many, this is a radical idea.

Dr. Parker emphasizes that harmonious relationships require awareness, not agreement. In fact, insisting on an agreement can be a hostile act. She indicates that the search for agreement can often lead to arguments because it invalidates the other person’s perspective, whereas the search for understanding dissolves the barriers that result in discord and harm and allows us to get to know one another.

According to recent reports, she explained it like this: “If I need to be right, then I’m not going to be able to listen to you unless you are in agreement with me. And, if I need to be right, it means either you have to agree with me or you’re wrong. The need to be right means that somebody else has to be wrong. Who likes to be wrong? Nobody. Nobody wants to be made to feel like they’re wrong. Making someone wrong will most likely push them into a protective stance. But, when we approach someone with curiosity, it creates a whole latest opening to make a connection with each other. We might say to them, ‘Tell me more…I’m really interested in that…I never thought about it that way.’”.

According to recent reports, when we are in difficult or uncomfortable conversations, can we create space to listen to each other with our differences? Can we create space for communication and connection for its own sake rather than for someone to be right and another to be wrong? How can we learn to understand each other rather than agree? How can we treat each other (and ourselves) better while learning to better understand each other and our different perspectives?

Pausing with the intention to prioritize Listening before speaking helps us regulate our nervous system so that we can not only create this space, but we are also less likely to activate someone else’s stress response. Khouri notes, “Imagine two nervous systems on high alert trying to have a conversation, it’s almost impossible! Especially if both parties are vying for being right. If you want to disrupt that pattern, you need to figure out how to self-regulate; part of that is about tolerating the discomfort of disagreeing with someone or being in conflict.”.

It has been revealed that “One of the most interesting things I’ve discovered in my work, is that when people feel really, really listened to, they themselves are more willing to try to understand the other person, even when they don’t agree,” continues Khouri. “Through this type of listening, I’ve seen some people with very strong convictions and beliefs loosen their grip on their own fixed ideas and start to open up their perspective or get greater understanding and empathy for a different perspective.”.

If we can Pause during a contentious situation and shift into curiosity, we might stay in the conversation long enough to ask questions that help us get to know someone, and listen in a way that makes them feel genuinely heard. When people feel heard and acknowledged, they are more likely to feel safe enough to listen in return. If we want to be heard and understood, it often starts with ensuring that the other person feels heard first. This of course takes practice.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that glute bridge post-run.
  • It has been revealed that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a new study on anti-movement vs.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that glute bridge post-run. (Photo: Aleksandr Kondratov, Getty).

It has been revealed that for this article, physical therapist Jennie Hansen analyzed a new study on anti-movement vs. dynamic core training and built a simple, science-backed core routine for runners based on the findings. The routine targets the deep stabilizing muscles that protect your spine and improve performance.

Recent findings suggest that “Core strengthening” is a term runners frequently toss around. We all know we need it. But what exactly is it, and what should it entail? (Hint: Not crunches.).

Recent findings suggest that when we talk about the core, we mean the abdominal muscles, low back, gluteal, pelvic, and hip muscles that support the spine and trunk. These muscles include both smaller, deep groups that attach directly to the spine to provide stabilization and larger, more global ones that can assist with stability and produce movement.

Why do we need this area to be strong? Well, even non-runners need to pay attention to their core strength to avoid lower back pain, which is the top cause of years lived with disability. Athletically, the core must create proximal stability to allow for powerful, efficient movements distally—which requires adequate strength combined with coordinated neuromuscular activation and control. So, core strength is certainly important for pain reduction, injury prevention, and athletic performance.

When running, the trunk serves to provide a stable base of support so that the legs can effectively generate the forces that create forward movement. These forces are transferred across the trunk and counterbalanced by the arms, requiring coordination between the hips, trunk muscles, and shoulders.

Sources indicate that while running appears to be purely a forward (sagittal plane) activity, the trunk muscles are hard at work controlling side-to-side (frontal plane) and rotational (transverse plane) forces. Muscle activation and timing change with speed, with higher speeds generally requiring more control and work. The deep trunk muscles also contribute to respiration.

It has been revealed that while some small trunk motion naturally occurs with running, excessive motion is detrimental. Increased trunk flexion is associated with decreased running economy and increased loading rates and vertical impact forces. Increased lateral trunk lean has also been linked to increased loading rates, which may play a role in the development of certain injuries.

Industry observers note that even though most of us know that crunches are out, there’s still plenty of confusion about how to train our cores. While strength work doesn’t need to look exactly like running, it does need to meet (and exceed) its demands—meaning that stability should be emphasized over motion.

It has been revealed that enter a recent study comparing neuromuscular activation between “anti-movement” and “dynamic” core training. Unlike traditional dynamic core exercises, which work the trunk and spinal musculature by moving through flexion, extension, rotation, and side bending, anti-movement exercises resist external forces, forcing stabilization throughout the trunk—basically, trunk isometrics.

The 12-week study compared a combination of Pallof holds and plank variations (incorporating bands and the TRX suspension trainer for progression) in the anti-movement program against a dynamic program that included exercises such as sit-ups, leg raises, jack knives, Russian twists, windshield wipers, and back extensions (incorporating Swiss balls for progression).

While both exercise groups demonstrated enhancements in neuromuscular efficiency compared to a control group, improvements were overall greater in the anti-movement group, particularly within the deep local musculature that activates prior to limb movement and plays an notable role in stabilizing the spine.

The authors therefore hypothesized that this enhanced neuromuscular efficiency could improve endurance, delay fatigue, and reduce the need for recruitment of larger, more global muscles—thus protecting the spine and potentially decreasing injury risk while improving performance.

Runners can apply these findings and consider an “anti-movement”-focused core routine, similar to the one used in the study. Nothing fancy or extensive is required—just one exercise each to resist the trunk’s motions (flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending/lateral flexion). Simple plank variations and other holds work well to streamline your core routine efficiently and effectively.

Targets: Anti-extension · full core (local and global).

The front plank is a classic core stability exercise that falls into the anti-extension category, challenging most of both the local and global core muscles.

Targets: Anti-flexion · spinal extensors and glutes.

While the study used a supine plank as its anti-flexion exercise, the shoulder position required could be a limiter, so bridge holds are likely a more practical way for many runners to work the posterior trunk muscles, including the spinal extensors and gluteals.

Targets: Anti-lateral flexion · lateral trunk and hip muscles.

The side plank can be considered an anti-lateral-flexion exercise, challenging the lateral trunk and hip musculature.

Targets: Anti-rotation · obliques and deep abdominal rotators.

The Pallof press is a common anti-rotation exercise, challenging the deep abdominal rotators, including the obliques.

#22487. What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1377 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1377 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again.
  • Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward.
  • Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, notes Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, notes Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

According to recent reports, keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try new fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy states. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”.

In a recent development, if you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

GET YOUR MAINTENANCE LOOKS HERE.

First, it’s crucial to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

Recent findings suggest that “The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” states Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

Sources indicate that then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy indicates. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

Industry observers note that this tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy notes.

Andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he says, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.).

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training initiative with relative ease.

It has been revealed that greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in Upcoming York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and plans to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

According to recent reports, retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more key than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he says, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”.

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:.

“The new race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy indicates. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”.

It has been revealed that sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is notable to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones indicates.

It has been revealed that laraia says one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

The maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones says. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still crucial to include one true rest day in your plan, Sheehy says.

Recent findings suggest that strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia says.

GET YOUR STRENGTH WORKOUTS HERE.

Laraia says signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

Sources indicate that still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he says. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a fresh training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

In a recent development, “Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia says. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.

'I Ran 3 Miles A Day For 21 Days—Here's What I Learned About My Brain And Body'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • It has been revealed that there’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run.
  • I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that there’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run. It’s simple. It’s gritty. It’s giving “I can do hard things just because I believe I can,” main character energy. Plus, running three miles a day has become a bit of a fitness trend lately—just scroll through TikTok and you’ll see thousands of people sticking to that sweet-spot distance to get in shape, clear their heads, or just establish a healthy daily habit.

I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent. So I challenged myself: Run (at least) three miles a day, every day, for three weeks—no skips. I wanted to see if this simple habit could actually deliver real results: Physically. Mentally. Emotionally. To cut to the chase, it did.

But before we dive into exactly what I learned, here’s what the challenge I set out for actually entailed: Each day, I carved out 30-ish minutes to run a minimum of three miles—sometimes on the treadmill, sometimes outside, depending on my mood (and the weather). Sometimes fast, sometimes slow—I wasn’t chasing speed, just consistency.

And while it started out as a little personal experiment, it turned into a full-on mindset shift that seeped into other areas of my life.

According to recent reports, I’m a pretty high-energy person, even on little sleep. And frankly, when I’m not exerting that physical energy enough during the day, I find it tough to settle down to sleep at night.

According to recent reports, by week two of this challenge, I was zonking out faster than usual and waking up feeling more rested. Research backs this up—moderate aerobic exercise like running can help you fall asleep quicker and improve sleep quality, per the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

There’s a reason running is considered a moving meditation (and I say this as someone who really struggles with stationary meditating). That ~30-minute mental break from work, life, communications, etc., helped me carve out time to shut off my brain and come back to reality with a fresh outlook.

Whatever I was stressing about before my run felt way less burdensome after taking time to move my body and just, well, not stress over that thing. I’d come back with more patience, more solutions, and frankly, a more can-do attitude about dealing with whatever was weighing me down before. My run became my reset button—and a way to make myself less irritable and more focused.

I’ve always gained (and lost) muscle pretty swiftly after starting or stopping a new exercise routine, however I typically first notice it around my abs and arms, as I'm leaner in those regions. So, when I saw my calves and quads popping a bit more in the mirror, and climbing the four flights of stairs up to my apartment started feeling easier than it used to, I knew my body was adapting. Even though I wasn’t lifting weights during this three week challenge (I tried to at first, but decided it was too much for my schedule while also running three miles daily), the repeated use of lower-body muscles while running led to strength gains.

Sources indicate that going into this challenge, I expected a mental impact of some sort (though I wasn’t quite sure what it would be), but I didn’t think my body would change much from a short-distance, short-term running habit. I already work out often (switching it up with two to three weekly strength training sessions, yoga/pilates once per week, and a two to five mile run once per week), so I didn’t think this challenge would have a palpable physical effect on me. So, the lower body muscle and strength gains were by far the most surprising benefit I walked away with.

I’d never really consider myself a “runner,” but doing it daily for three weeks made the act feel less intimidating and more second nature to me. A study in Psychology of Sport and Exercise reveals that consistency in movement creates more positive attitudes toward the habit, which makes you more likely to keep showing up. My experience totally backed that up.

It has been revealed that around day six, I felt myself gearing up for my run more instinctually—getting dressed, grabbing my headphones, keys, and lacing up my sneakers just right without having to think about it much. If on the first few runs I was moseying around the neighborhood walking for several blocks to put off actually starting the run, by week two I was excitedly hitting the pavement at my three-mile pace almost as soon as I got outside. Pacing myself began to feel more natural without checking my Nike Run Club app, and I started tapping into the sound of my feet hitting the concrete to gauge my effort.

Recent findings suggest that before this challenge, I had a habit of engaging in pretty critical self-talk on the regular. Also, mentally checking out mid-run was the norm in order to just get through it. My internal monologue when running used to be all about how much time was left, how uncomfortable I felt, or how nice it would feel to just stop. But sticking to a daily running habit triggered the kind of awareness and shift of self-talk that I’d been long overdue for. That mindset shift was probably the biggest win of all.

After a few days of three miles under my belt, I started celebrating tiny wins—like not stopping on a hill or picking up my pace on the final stretch. Instead of counting down the minutes or fixating on how slow I was moving, I was hyping myself up, which only propelled me further. Whether it was a solo sunset jog or a playlist-powered treadmill sesh, I always felt a little lighter—and a little more capable of not just enduring, but thriving through hard things—post-run. That energy and positive shift in self-talk started showing up in how I talked to myself outside of workouts, too.

It’s wild how one habit tends to have a domino effect, whether it’s constructive or destructive. Once I started running every day, I realized I wanted to support that effort outside of my run window. That meant reaching for water instead of a second coffee, getting in some light stretching at night, prioritizing protein in my meals, and actually winding down for sleep earlier than usual instead of binge-watching or doom-scrolling.

According to recent reports, the momentum from running made other wellness choices feel less like chores and more like natural choices for self-care. I wasn’t trying to overhaul my entire routine overnight, but these little tweaks felt pretty intuitive, and really added up to help me stick with the challenge, and feel more energized and clear-headed throughout the day.

Industry observers note that okay, so full transparency: I didn’t just wake up one day and bust out 21 straight three-milers. I eased in by starting off slow to establish a new routine, and listening to my body along the way. Here’s how to start running three miles a day—without burning out.

Pro tip: “If you’re just starting out, alternate running days with walking or strength training to let your body adjust,” run coach Corky Corkum, CPT, previously told WH. “The number one reason new runners quit is injury or burnout from doing too much too soon.”.

Sources indicate that want to try running three miles a day for yourself? These things made all the difference:.

If your goal is to feel stronger, sleep better, and just feel a little more capable and confident—all with minimal equipment or cost—then yes, 100 percent. You don’t need a marathon medal to call yourself a runner or to be consistent. You just need a pair of sneakers, a bit of stick-to-it-ness, and a willingness to start where you are.

And if you happen to find yourself romanticizing the idea of making a daily jog a habit? I say lean into it.

Latest Update: The Unexpected Benefits of Doing Inversions in Yoga

(Photo: Andrew Clark | Design in Canva by Laura Harold).

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about the effects of inversions in yoga first appeared in the November-December 1983 matter of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here. You can also read more about inversions.

Sources indicate that the Headstand and Shoulderstand positions, Sirsasana and Sarvangasana, have long been known as the king and queen of the asanas. By reversing the body’s usual relationship to gravity, these asanas produce numerous beneficial changes in the body’s physiological systems. Because there are also many additional physical, psychological, and emotional benefits that come with the practice of these poses, they are often considered the core of a complete asana practice. However, to truly experience their benefits and prevent injury, they must be done correctly.

What are the effects of reversing the gravitational pull on the human body and why is it desirable? Are there dangers and precautions to working with inversions, and what are the safest ways to work with gravity? These are questions all of us may have asked, and with the recent backlash against inversions, they deserve a full discussion.

All posture and movement must take into account the constant downward pulling force of gravity. Our bones provide some support and resistance, but fluids, which compromise 75 to 80 percent of our mass, are at the mercy of the “big G.” Just as water always flows downhill, the liquids in our body flow down the gravitational gradient, and the circulatory system must constantly adjust to gravity’s effects.

It has been revealed that in “Effects of Inverted Poses on Cardiovascular Physiology,” IYTE Review, Vol. 3, #3, Marcia Stefanick, Ph.D., details these adjustments. As the body changes its relationship to gravity, she writes, “profound changes occur in the distribution of blood in the vessels and the return of blood to the heart, as well as in the heart rate and blood pressure.” The cardiovascular system is composed of the heart and blood vessels. The heart consists of two separate pumps. One pumps blood into the lungs where carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen. This fresh blood returns to the heart and the second pump squeezes it out to the body.

Sources indicate that the blood flows outward through large vessels known as arteries, which in turn branch and subdivide into the smaller and smaller vessels that wind their way to every organ and tissue in the body. At the level of the smallest vessels, the capillaries, the oxygen and other nutrients and messengers leave the blood stream and are transported to the cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide and other metabolic wastes are absorbed into the blood stream. This deoxygenated blood flows from the capillaries into larger vessels (venules), which lead to the still larger veins that return the blood to the heart, where the cycle begins again.

Because some of the unwanted cell waste material is too large to be absorbed through the tiny pores in the walls of the capillaries, a second set of vessels, the lymphatic system, transports excess cellular fluid as well as large protein molecules, dead cell matter, bacteria and other material. Before being recycled back into the blood stream near the heart, this fluid is filtered by the lymph nodes, which are located at critical junctures along the lymphatic system network. At these points, dead cells and particles are absorbed, bacteria are attacked and digested, and toxins are neutralized. Thus, the lymphatic system plays a key role in guarding the body against infection and in maintaining overall health.

It has been revealed that one of the most vital functions of the cardiovascular system is to deliver fresh blood to the brain. In lying-down positions, the heart is at the same level as the brain, and gravity has a minor effect on the movement of blood between these two organs. In sitting or standing, however, the brain is obviously above the heart and the heart muscle must work intensely to pump against the pull of gravity. In an inverted position, the brain is below the level of the heart and gravity pulls blood into the brain. In these positions, the brain receives the proper blood supply with the minimum effort of the heart.

Recent findings suggest that tests done by Shanker Rao, as described in Science Studies Yoga by James Funderburk, show how the heart rate varies with gravity. His subjects, medical students with some experience in yoga, exhibited an average heart rate of 67 beats per minute in the supine position, rising to 84 beats per minute upon standing. In the Headstand position, these subjects displayed a 69 beats-per-minute average. This heart rate variation was accomplished by a variation in fluid pressure in the arteries, veins, glands and organs. The regular increase in pressure in the head, neck and chest regions brought about by inversions maintains the elasticity of the vessels and tissues, and it is this elasticity that is a key factor in maintaining health.

According to recent reports, just as it affects arterial blood flow, gravity affects the flow of venous blood back to the heart. There are three ways in which the deoxygenated blood can be returned to the heart. The first is gravity, which will drain the region above the heart of the venous blood and lymphatic fluid, but will resist the return of fluids from the lower body. The second two mechanisms, the respiratory pump and the skeletal musculature, must do all the work of returning the fluids below the heart. The changing pressure in the thoracic cavity, which pulls air into the lungs, pulls fluids toward the heart. Exhalations are quite notable in this respiratory pumping action. Also, the contraction and releasing of the skeletal muscles serve to pump the venous and lymphatic fluids through their respective vessels. These vessels are equipped with a series of one-way valves that allow blood to flow toward the heart only, thus preventing backflow.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, these two mechanisms cannot compete against gravity for long periods of time. During the course of a typical day, most humans will spend 16 or more hours with the head above the heart and the legs and the pelvic area below. Thus, gravity has a negative effect on the venous and lymphatic return from most of the body, and if the muscles of the legs are not continuously contracting and releasing, fluid begins to accumulate in the lower body. This will almost always occur where there is not much opportunity for movement.

It has been revealed that because the veins and lymphatic vessels are quite elastic, they can expand to hold large quantities of fluid, but, if not given periodic relief from this pooling, the vessels eventually lose their resilience to become permanently distended. The one-way valves then break down from over-stretching and varicose veins result. (Inversions can alleviate the problems of varicose veins, and, if begun in time, can prevent them.) Periodic inversions allow gravity to drain the lower body, relieving pressure and recycling the lymphatic fluid and venous blood. This in turn gives the cells a continuous supply of fresh nutrients and cleanses them of metabolic wastes. An efficient circulatory system, so vital to health, is thus maintained and improved by inversions.

In a recent development, as we have seen, there are many tremendous benefits to be gained by inverting the body. However, it is equally important to be aware of the potential dangers involved in inverted positions. Needless to say, everyone should check with their before beginning any physical regimen. Furthermore, it is always wise to be cautious and work into things slowly.

Certain groups of people should avoid all inversions except when working under the most expert guidance. Those with high blood pressure are one such group, since the cardiovascular changes of inversions are potentially damaging to them. Under the supervision of a physician or an experienced yoga teacher, some people with high blood pressure may be able to do some inversions, but this is not an area to be explored by the average student or teacher. Other people who should avoid inversions are those who experience certain eye conditions—such as glaucoma or detached retina—hiatal hernia, heart or stroke problems, epilepsy, seizures or other brain disorders, and spinal injury (except when inversions are used as part of a supervised therapy program).

Certain temporary conditions also prohibit the practice of inversions. People are advised not to practice inversions during the menstrual period, and inversions during pregnancy should be practiced only by experienced students working with an experienced teacher. Active inversions should also be avoided by older people with osteoporosis, especially those with a history of vertebral fractures.

Triathlon as the New Run Club: Community Without “Bro Culture”

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities.
  • According to recent reports, what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon?
  • From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Triathlon club founders and disruptors share how they are building inclusive communities. (Photo: Courtesy Alexa and Branden Scheel, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson, Hannah Bradbury, Hilary Topper, and Kyla Lupo).

According to recent reports, what do you do when you’re fed up with the elitism that can lurk in various pockets of triathlon? You could throw up your hands in defeat and frustration over the bro culture and inclusion challenges, vowing to train in solitude like a spandex-clad, multisport monk. Or … you could start your own tri club, team, group ride, or clinic.

From free 140.6-mile races and no-drop rides to psychic readings and book clubs (and more book clubs), meet the tri club disruptors who are daring to shake up triathlon by prioritizing inclusion, whole health, and social connection over watts, body exclusivity, and snobbery.

When Altitude Multisport Club, a tri club in Denver, Colorado, was founded in 2010, the board consisted of all men.

“While friendly, it had a very ‘bro’ vibe and club events were rarely organized by leadership and club meetings were salesy,” says Erin Trail, Altitude Multisport Club’s former president and current volunteer. “What did it for me was a no-drop group ride that the current president and coaching director were on. I had done three Ironman races, and they dropped ME. I knew the route and was fine, but I thought: ‘What if I was a upcoming person? What kind of experience would this be?’”.

Since the president was term-limited, Trail was able to step up as president in 2016 to change the atmosphere to a friendlier, more inclusive one.

In a recent development, “That first year was very hard. I decided to make the club more inclusive and friendly to beginners and women, eliminating sales or conflict of interest issues and improving communications,” Trail notes. “I lost a LOT of club friends because I wanted to make things different. Half my board quit because they didn’t want to be held accountable. But in my first year as president, membership grew from 50 to 150 members!”.

Today, Altitude Multisport Club features winter Sunday pool swims with a coach and travel camps to Moab and a local state park in addition to regular training and racing activities.

“My second term as president was much better, with a diverse board that I handpicked. We added a family membership so households, including kids, could join at a group rate,” Trail says. “And we made it clear that the environment is welcoming, organized, and a safe space to learn for everyone.”.

“A LOT of skinny white men. That’s what I saw in triathlon. I didn’t see enough women, and I really didn’t see anyone who was bigger. I realized that if I wanted to see more folks that looked like me, I had to be the coach that made triathlon a place for all folks, regardless of size, shape, color, or anything else,” states Kyla Lupo, who took things into her own hands, getting certified as a coach, learning everything she could, and starting her team, Go Major!, with just one athlete and “a bunch of friends pretending to be my team.” Since then, Go Big! has grown to 22 athletes.

“Our team makes a point to let folks know that they are already loved, exactly as they are. Team Go Substantial! stands for a radical level of body inclusivity, both in sport and the world,” Kyla notes. “On Team Go Big!, we work to overcome our fear and doubts while getting fit and ready for the start line. Anyone can tri in the body they have right now.”.

Social connection is crucial to the Go Significant! community and takes the form of weekly team meetings where members from around the country learn, share their goals, ask for support, and expect accountability.

It has been revealed that “We are from all over the country, but there’s a Tuesday morning virtual trainer ride to further connect us. And of course we get to party together at races,” Lupo states.

Disruptors: Alexa and Branden Scheel.

People often join tri clubs to find community, only to discover that they are a small fish in a massive sea. When you’re one of hundreds of athletes, you and your journey can get lost in the mix.

It has been revealed that “My husband, Branden, and I were part of two different teams like that. We felt like ‘just another membership,’” Alexa Scheel states.

So she and Branden pursued certifications from USA Triathlon and began building the kind of team they actually wanted to be part of. In 2023, the Scheels released Branden Scheel Racing, which focuses on athlete relationships and connection. Despite being a team with athletes around the world, the Scheels strive to make their team feel like family and make each athlete feel seen.

In a recent development, “If we don’t personally know something about each of the team members, we’ve grown too major, which is why we sit between 100 to 150 members. We are committed to keeping this team on the smaller side,” Scheel says. The beating heart of the team is its Facebook group, where athletes connect through monthly games and seminars, get answers to their most pressing questions, and find encouragement.

It has been revealed that “On our team, every athlete stays until the last athlete completes their event because EVERYONE deserves to have someone cheering them on at the finish line. We’ve even had 15 people stay at the finish line for the midnight finish of Ironman Arizona for one of our athletes,” Scheel says. “Having a tri family on and off course to cheer for you and celebrate one of the best days of your life is a huge part of our team culture.”.

Disruptors: Jaclyn Fahey, Tara Hofmayer, and Sami Saad.

Fifteen years ago, Jaclyn Fahey started a tri team through a bike store. As it evolved, Fahey recognized the need for a more affordable Long Island-based team, and Landshark Endurance was born.

According to recent reports, “It began as a pizza-and-beer team with a triathlon problem, but Tara and Sami have helped take the lead. Because both are speech therapists and have the gift of gab, they’ve attracted a lot more members,” Fahey says. The open-level, co-ed multisport team supports members of all backgrounds with educational clinics and workshops, group workouts, and of course, social events that revolve around pizza and beer.

Sources indicate that “By sharing our passion and experiences, we hope to show young athletes that success isn’t always measured by winning, but by perseverance, sportsmanship, and the courage to try,” Fahey says. “You don’t have to be the fastest or the strongest. You just have to show up for yourself, put in the effort, and enjoy the journey. At the end of the day, the greatest part isn’t always crossing the finish line – it’s the people who help you get there.”.

Sources indicate that “I’m non-binary, and when I visit online triathlon groups and ask if there are any fellow non-binary athletes, it’s not uncommon that transphobes will flood the comments. I can only speak for myself, but the fear of discrimination, or being attacked verbally or worse, can be the most intimidating thing for non-binary and trans triathletes about tri clubs,” notes Ruth Carter, a lawyer and triathlete. “There’s so much misinformation out there about trans women and non-binary athletes, as well as assumptions that are not supported by research.”.

When Carter couldn’t find a triclub that promoted equal participation and respect, they created Mutants & Masochists, a tri club that believes in equal participation, recognition, and respect for all triathletes, and advocates for non-binary and trans triathletes.

“We’re just getting started, but I hope the club is a place where trans people can connect, both online and in real life,” Carter indicates.

In 2023, Hannah Bradbury was training to break an open-water swim record when she was rushed to the ER for an emergency surgery to remove her gallbladder.

“My first thought when I woke up was, ‘When can I get back in the water?’ The answer was six weeks at least,” notes Bradbury, who had already lost half of her thyroid to cancer in 2017. In an attempt to be part of sport in a way that cancer or a freak surgery couldn’t disrupt, Bradbury created Chicago’s North Avenue Swim and Triathlon Yo (NASTY) Instagram account to post about swimming until she could get back in the water. She also released book clubs and threw happy hours to create space for people to be more than just athletes, from cancer survivors to diabetic athletes striving to stay in sport on their own terms.

Sources indicate that “Tri and swim clubs are great at training people. They’re not always great at holding onto people when they’re injured, sick, slow, starting over, or just burned out. I wanted to build a club that could hold everyone, from those winning the Chicago Triathlon to anyone rebuilding from injuries, or battling setbacks and the identity crises nobody warns you about when you’re sidelined,” states Bradbury, who faced another cancer scare in 2023. “While I waited on the biopsy, my friends kept me distracted by doing a 100-mile ride with me, covered in glitter, that we called the ride Centuslay.”.

Fortunately, the biopsy came back negative, and the women’s century became an official NASTY tradition every fall.

“Before NASTY I had a hard time making real friends with people who don’t just ask, ‘How was your swim?’ Through NASTY, I met friends who ask how they can show up for me,” Bradbury indicates. “NASTY has grown to over 340 members, and through this community, people have found jobs through a swim or a random happy hour, and even fallen in love. Sport has become an accessory to our friendships, not the glue.”.

“When I first got into triathlon in 2010, I was fortunate to have a warm, welcoming entry point into the sport. My goal with the T2 community is to pay it forward so others can also ease into the sport, learn to love it, and stay connected for the long haul,” says Bryan Mewes, who opened T2 Triathlon & Cycling, a triathlon-focused bike shop in Long Beach, California, in 2023. “The biggest hurdle for beginners is usually being overwhelmed by gear. That and the open-water swim. Once they realize that the shop is a space where they can comfortably ask questions and our group is built on encouragement rather than competition, that anxiety disappears fast.”.

Mewes explains that while it’s easy to say “everyone is welcome,” making sure someone is paired up with a partner at their pace or ensuring no one gets left behind takes actual effort that T2’s committed to making. Beyond the group rides, weekly runs, and bay swims, T2 brings people together off the course and keeps the vibe low-key and welcoming by hosting family dinners at local restaurants, beach days after races, and even a movie club.

“Some people only do our social events, while others only join our rides. What matters is that they participate in their way and see themselves as part of the community. That’s the core of T2. Training is just the anchor,” Mewes notes.

Disruptors: Ruth Marie Oliver and Team Rocket’s Race Directors and Officers.

Team Rocket Tri Club (TRTC) is on a mission to promote a fit and healthy lifestyle. Every month, the club organizes a themed, post-brick social, and throughout the year, it hosts various races, from a beginner-friendly pool swim to a duathlon and sprint triathlons.

It has been revealed that during the summer months, TRTC hosts Tuesday night bricks featuring a multitude of pace groups, ensuring no rider is left behind and everyone has buddies to ride with. And in the winter, the focus is on swim clinics and winter trail running.

“Our club president, Ruth Marie Oliver, has done amazing things, including growing our membership to over 300 people,” says Cynthia Mitchell, race director of TRTC’s Heel and Crank Duathlon.

In a recent development, to up the fun factor, TRTC has its own well-traveled bike box that members can borrow, adding their own sticker to its travel history and essentially bringing the whole team along for that athlete’s adventure. There’s also a TRTC hat that is currently “on tour.” It’s been spotted everywhere from Leeds, Alabama, to the head of Bob Babbit in Kona during the Ironman World Championship this year.

Disruptors: Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson.

In 2019, Corinne Geerdts Merten and Melissa Niemuth-Seamonson relaunched TriBabes WI, a women’s-only, USAT-certified team, to provide a community for women of all abilities and ages to train together.

Industry observers note that “Some women join us purely to have the chance to work out with others for one, two, or all three sports. No matter what the sport or goal, we support each other without all the egos,” Merten claims. TriBabesWI makes aspects of triathlon like climbing hills, changing tires, nutrition, and making a race strategy less daunting through the clinics it offers. For TriBabe’s annual team triathlon, athletes can ride with a buddy for the bike portion.

Team offerings aren’t limited to the swim-bike-run. There are team hikes, skiing and snowshoeing in the winter, and opportunities to volunteer and shake a cowbell for others.

“We’ve donated our time and efforts to Breakthrough T1D, USAT triathlon events in Milwaukee, Ironman Wisconsin, and naturally Girls on the Run,” Merten says.

In a recent development, “When I was new to this sport, I went for a bike ride with a triathlon group and got dropped within moments,” says Topper, an author and coach who started WeREndurance in 2017. “If you’re just starting out, don’t look like everyone else, or just feel different from everyone, many clubs can feel elitist, especially when you get dropped. WeREndurance is nothing like that. It’s inclusive and diverse.”.

As the group’s triathletes grew older and more injury-prone, however, WeREndurance membership began to drop, so Topper proposed transitioning from a strictly triathlon group to a lifestyle group. Now, WeREndurance members who live locally in Long Beach, Upcoming York, can participate in monthly hikes and quarterly races, as well as pool parties, holiday parties, diner breakfasts, and even a psychic night. Members who live out of state can stay connected through monthly meditation sessions, a book club, and monthly/bi-monthly educational webinars.

Industry observers note that “These types of activities welcome everyone, including those who are injured or on the sidelines. This builds bonds and social connections,” Topper explains. “As you get older, you realize that sport is not only about being on the podium. It’s about community and having fun with your peers. The social aspect becomes just as crucial as training and racing.”.

Disruptors: Brian Masayon, David Bahia, and Kristoffer Crisostomo.

In 2017, Masayon, Crisostomo, Bahia, and six of their friends formed a “silly” club to make training fun, and in doing so, others began taking notice.

“People started reaching out, asking how to join the team. I replied that there was no team. After the 20th inquiry or so, the nine of us decided to open 3P TRI to the public as a fun, drama-free group. That was in October 2017. By the end of the year, we had over 120 members join,” Masayon says. As word spread, the nonprofit tri club’s inclusive vibe attracted members from Canada, Australia, the Philippines, and Mexico.

While Ironman race entries cost athletes between $900 and $1,200, 3P TRI has removed the financial barrier entirely, offering clinics and free 140.6-mile races that are fully supported by the team.

Sources indicate that “There is no timing chip, so members are not pressured to prove how fast or slow they are. Instead, they train and then enjoy race day with their teammates,” Masayon indicates. For 3P’s 140.6 triathlon, members come from different states to volunteer and help their teammates finish.

“People are intimidated by tri clubs because they have this impression of triathletes as being fast, quick, and strong. Our members, however, come in all shapes and sizes, and this becomes an inspiration to many people,” Masayon adds. “Nobody talks about speed and ability. We don’t play the comparison game.”.

Five years ago, a group of Newly introduced Jersey moms tried a mud run. They had so much fun that one run turned into a road race, followed by group bike rides, and finally dipping their nail-less toes into triathlons, despite the level of intimidation.

It has been revealed that “At a 5K, you’ll see everyone from Boston qualifiers to families participating together, sometimes with little kids in tow. Triathlons can seem like a different world from road or obstacle races. They require training and preparation across three disciplines, and the level of athleticism on display can be intimidating. Sometimes it feels like there are no actual beginners, just really accomplished athletes with super fancy bikes,” claims Merino, adding that if someone demonstrates up to ride with a mountain bike, they probably know it’s not the fastest option and don’t necessarily need unsolicited advice about upgrading. The same goes for swim form, running technique, or anything else. “If someone asks for pointers, we absolutely help them! Otherwise, the most encouraging thing we can do may be simply making them feel like they belong.”.

“That’s what Team Thunderclap is all about. We might not have the fanciest gear or be the fastest people, but we show up, give it everything we’ve got, and probably laugh a whole lot along the way,” Merino states. “At the end of the day, most of us aren’t competing for Olympic medals. We’re ordinary people doing extraordinary things in our spare time.”.

A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

  • "Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

Industry observers note that the Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and Upcoming York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

Sources indicate that as far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

Sources indicate that in a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and stated she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the Latest York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex.".

According to recent reports, her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified.".

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sager said she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing prepares, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:.

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ.".

Industry observers note that sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#22476. Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist
