Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Industry observers note that nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run.
  • While this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run. Then winter arrives, the temperatures drop, and suddenly it’s three straight months of daily prerun procrastination: I look for any excuse, task, or chore to delay heading out into the cold or stepping on the treadmill.

While this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run. Except by then, I’m crunched for time, it’s pitch-black outside, and the whole process has drained enough of my mental energy that I’d rather push those miles to tomorrow.

I know I’m not alone: Even professional marathoners fall into the “run-crastination” spiral. Previously, Des Linden and Kara Goucher discussed their own experiences on their podcast, Nobody Asked Us with Des & Kara. Still, I’d much rather find a way to avoid getting sucked in so I can get on with my run and my day, and enjoy both a little more as a result.

So, I asked a sports psychologist what actually works to get you out the door in the winter when anything sounds better than a run—plus when it’s actually a better idea to skip the miles.

The first step to beating prerun procrastination? Determine the reason you’re doing it. “Procrastination is usually one of two things,” Justin Ross, Psy.D., a clinical sports psychologist and UESCA-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “One: It’s an avoidance strategy, because what you’re about to do is uncomfortable, unpleasant, hard, or challenging. But, it can also signal toward a different need that’s not being met.”.

In the winter months—especially for driven runners coming off a fall marathon season—that other need can be rest. “True athletic wisdom is knowing the difference between when procrastination is avoidance, and when it’s a sign that you need something other than a run that day,” Ross explains.

Gaining that wisdom as an athlete takes time, practice, and some trial and error. The best way to start? Focus on creating “systems” that make procrastination less likely so you can more easily identify the action that aligns with your needs, goals, and values, Ross says. Most times, these systems (which we outline below) lead to better outcomes than trying to rely on willpower alone or following an impulse in the moment.

If you find yourself avoiding a run, remove as many obstacles as possible that stand between you and getting out the door or to the gym. For Ross, that means setting out all his running clothes and fuel ahead of time so he doesn’t need to hunt for that one pair of gloves he hasn’t seen since last January.

“Without preparation, procrastination becomes a whole lot easier because you have all these extra hurdles,” he explains. “When it’s dark and cold in the winter, you need to problem-solve in ways that you don’t need to when it’s beautiful out and you’re excited to run.”.

For me, that means making sure my headlamp actually has working batteries if I’m planning to run outside in the evenings. If I’m hitting the treadmill, I cue up a playlist, TV show, or podcast on my phone and stock my gym bag with a postrun snack and a full water bottle.

It has been revealed that when you’re procrastinating a run, try shifting your focus from what you’re doing to why you’re doing it. “Remind yourself why this run is notable to you or how it helps you,” Ross notes. For example, you might think about your values or current goals and consider how this workout brings you closer to them.

I’ve found I’m motivated simply by the fact that running makes me feel like my favorite version of myself—and that boosts my mood more than any race-specific or fitness goal. But you might be more excited by the idea that staying consistent with your training over the winter will set you up for a stronger chance at a marathon PR in the spring.

Sources indicate that consider what might add a little bit more spark to your routine or make it more enticing. You might decide to meet up with a friend or local run club for a few miles. You might look forward to your treadmill run as “the 30 minutes of my day where I don’t have to be bothered and I can just watch my favorite show [alone],” says Ross.

The reward mindset helps you refocus on what brings you joy, instead of just relieving the pressure of needing to get in a workout.

Another helpful strategy? Doing the absolute bare minimum. “Runners often fall into this trap of having rigid rules around their exercise or their training,” says Ross. Try letting go of whatever mileage or workout you had planned for the day, and tell yourself that you’ll just run for 10 minutes and then reassess how you feel.

According to recent reports, you may even want to adjust your whole training standard ahead of the winter season, Ross says. For example, you might reduce the length, intensity, or frequency of the workouts you strategy to do each week. Or, instead of targeting a specific pace or mileage requirement, run or cross-train solely based on time. “Think about being more flexible in your approach during the winter months. Maybe you aim for the minimal effective dose to get the benefit you’re looking for, like just running for 20 minutes if your usual standard is 60,” Ross suggests.

It has been revealed that ross explains that winter can be a meaningful time for runners to examine what rules they have around their training that might be adding pressure. For example, I used to follow a silly rule from an old college teammate who remarked that any run shorter than three miles “didn’t count” as a true run. Once I finally let go of that, I found it much easier to get moving—even if it was just for an easy walk in the park near my house.

“This time of year, see how you can approach exercise from an overall health or mood-boost perspective instead of a training perspective,” suggests Ross.

Also, question any rigid rules you’ve established for yourself around volume, pace, or mileage—like making sure to hit a specific number of miles every week or setting a minimum pace requirement for all your runs—because they may backfire and lead to mental burnout over the long term, he notes.

It has been revealed that if you’ve done all the above and you still can’t get yourself out the door, a run may not actually be what you need. “If you keep hitting the moment to head out and that intuitive voice says, ‘I just really don’t want to,’ try listening to that voice. Listen to your body,” Ross suggests. “It’s okay to give yourself permission for rest and recovery—especially during this time of year.”.

Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

Fashion Has Entered Its Running Era

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • There was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run.
  • In a recent development, running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly new (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run. They were sweaty and wearing sneakers that looked like they belonged exclusively on a track. These days, the shoes tell you almost nothing. That guy wearing carbon-plated racers might be heading out for a tempo run, or he might just be on his way to a bar or running errands (in a casual fit).

In a recent development, running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly new (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different. Instead of reviving old silhouettes, fashion brands are getting their hands on actual performance shoes, and, frankly, some of the results are pretty damn good.

Take Adidas' collaboration with Satisfy, the Parisian running brand that's become something of a cult favorite among runners who lowkey like to look good while out and about. Earlier this year, the two brands gave the Adizero Adios Pro 4 a makeover, swapping its usual racing aesthetic for earthy tones, spray-painted details, and metallic accents. At first glance, they look like something you could spot on an edgy Instagram campaign, perhaps even a fashion week after-party in Bushwick, depending on the outfit. Except, it's still a legitimate racing shoe with Lightstrike Pro foam and EnergyRods. You could absolutely chase a PR in these. Whether you'd want to get them dirty is another question. That’s just merely scraping the surface, though.

It has been revealed that highsnobiety's latest collaboration with Saucony takes a similar approach, but with two very different sneakers: the Endorphin Pro 5, made for racing, and the ProGrid Paramount, a retro-inspired shoe that's more at home on city streets. Both get a modest makeover that makes technical sneakers look good with practically anything. Some of you probably appreciate the distinction here: one shoe is built for runners, and the other is for people who strictly care about style.

Then there's Hoka x Marni, which might be one of my favorites of the bunch. After giving the Bondi a ridiculously puffy, almost cartoonish makeover in 2025, the brands returned this November with the Clifton Marni, a more wearable take on Hoka's Clifton 11. There are metallic details, reflective accents, and a plaid sockliner, but underneath it all is still the cushioned daily trainer runners already know. It's stylish without looking like it's trying too hard, which can't be remarked for every designer sneaker collaboration.

It has been revealed that other brands have been getting in on the fun, too. Salomon and Pas Normal Studios recently put their spin on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL, giving the gravel running shoe a sleek, outdoorsy look while keeping its GORE-TEX protection and trail-ready outsole. Aimé Leon Dore has brought its signature New York aesthetic to New Balance's FuelCell Rebel v5 and SC Elite v5, while Nike tapped designer Melitta Baumeister to reimagine the Vomero Premium and Pegasus Premium. Even Loewe and On are experimenting with high-fashion versions of technical running shoes. By now, the crossover is hard to ignore.

Sources indicate that of course, there's something funny about running, a sport that really doesn't require much beyond a decent pair of shoes (and your ability to actually run, of course), becoming another excuse to buy expensive, limited-edition sneakers. And not that this has to be mentioned, but a designer collaboration isn't automatically a better running shoe. The fit, cushioning, and performance still matter, especially if you're planning to do more than walk around in them. But I do think it's cool that brands are putting this much thought into how performance footwear looks. Running clothes have gotten a lot more stylish in recent years, so why shouldn't the shoes follow?

Josiah Soto is a commerce editor and writer at Hearst Magazines, where he covers skincare, grooming, beauty, and style for Men’s Health, Prevention, and BestProducts.com. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first time I entered the Upcoming York City Marathon drawing, I got in. I’m not sure what possessed me that day to apply, having never run another race in my life. I figured I’d never get in, so why not? I played soccer growing up, and when the world shut down during COVID-19, running became the easiest way to get out of the house and see my friends. That’s where my running journey began.

According to recent reports, my NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges. While I was excited to run, I also didn’t want to miss out on any of the socializing that happened that year. I did my best to make it to every party, every club soccer game, and anything in between while running as much as possible. I was scared that running was going to infringe on my everyday life and I wouldn’t have time to keep having fun. Despite all of that, I had caught the marathon bug and after finishing the Fresh York City Marathon in 2022, I went on to run the Paris and Chicago Marathons in 2024.

In a recent development, while training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real blueprint, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar. My strategy consisted of building up mileage in order to reach 20 miles about four weeks out from race day. In between, I pieced together training information from influencers on Instagram and Google searches (this was pre-ChatGPT!). Now that I’m a Runner’s World+ member, I have all those resources right at my fingertips.

Although I caught the marathon bug almost instantly, I also felt defeated after New York. I knew I could have done better. Between New York City in 2022 and Paris in 2024, I never ran more than 10 miles at a time, but I was running enough that I knew I could do it again if I really wanted. I followed a similar approach for Chicago in 2024: Build up to one long run about a month out, then fill the rest of the weeks with shorter runs and one medium-length run. It wasn’t much of a proposal, but it worked for me. My times kept improving, and I broke four hours for the first time in Chicago.

It has been revealed that looking back, I realize that my no-initiative approach was partly a way to protect myself. If I never said my goal out loud, I couldn’t feel disappointed if I missed it. Breaking four hours in Chicago changed that. For the first time, I wanted to see what I could do with a real plan.

I was now living in the city I had expected to call home ever since I left college, so I really wanted this race to feel meaningful. For the first time in my marathon career, I downloaded a Runner’s World training strategy, the 16-week Break 3:45 plan to be exact, printed it out, and started tracking all of my runs. I wanted to beat my time in Chicago and get as close to 3 hours and 45 minutes as possible.

In the beginning, this felt super daunting. I had never done an interval run in my life nor had I ever intentionally sought out hills to make my runs feel harder than they already did. Nonetheless, I found my old Garmin Forerunner 55 and learned how to upload intervals to run up and down the West Side Highway. When the plan called for hills, I made my way back to the Queensboro Bridge for the first time since 2022, ready to face it with excitement instead of fear. Even while pretending to be excited, the incline is no joke!

Industry observers note that for a while, I really felt like I had gotten the hang of things. I actually started to recognize what different paces felt like during the intervals, instead of sprinting and pulling back and looking at my watch while I ran. And, I could now confidently run over many of the bridges in Newly introduced York City, notably the Williamsburg and Manhattan, even though they aren’t even part of the marathon course. I wasn’t following the plan exactly, but I was able to reorganize the days of the week to hit all the workouts.

This was working! Until it wasn’t.

Near the end of August (roughly week eight of the initiative), it became hot all the time, I was constantly traveling for weekend trips, and I had started to lose the excitement of running. So while I was making sure to hit all of the long runs, the interval training fell off completely. I was a little disappointed in myself because the interval training runs were workouts that made me feel like I was getting stronger each week. I had never done this type of workout before, so I could tell I was getting better each time.

Industry observers note that to find the joy of running again, I really started to lean on my friends. Every week, I’d send out a few texts to see who was available and wanted to go for a run with me. I ran the loop in Central Park almost every week and met up with my friends in Brooklyn to run every Friday morning. I started to explore parts of the city I had never been to before, which helped ground me in my training and remember that running is supposed to be fun and is an exciting way to explore the city.

From my previous experience, I knew that running the long runs was the most notable thing for me to feel confident on race day. So much of marathon running is mental, so knowing that I could run 20 miles (and have run 26.2 before), was enough for me. So, while I started with a plan, I started reverting back to my tried-and-true method—the just make sure you run the long runs plan.

Outside of the training initiative itself, I leaned on Runner’s World a lot. I didn’t have access to this in the past so I didn’t feel confident about planning for prerun meals or even how to take gels during the race. I also found that being able to read runner stories online made me feel more connected to the community, which helped me mentally with my training.

It has been revealed that initiative or no plan, I’m proud of myself! My official time was 3:57:39, so while I did not achieve my goal of breaking 3:45, I did run a sub-4 race, and following the Runner’s World plan helped me get there. The last time I ran this race, I was a senior in college and thought I had it all figured out. I was going to move to New York City, get a real adult job, and start the life I had been imagining. Similar to my experience following the Runner’s World plan, this is not how everything went. Instead, I moved to a different city after graduating, eventually found my way back to New York, and my life is so much more full than I ever expected because of it. Maybe things aren’t always supposed to go to plan, and that’s a good thing!

#22473. Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1063 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Triathlete ↗ Open Full Page

Reviewed: The EZ Hydro-Glide Swim Cap

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone.
  • In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.
  • Before we dive into the science, an crucial clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jumping into frigid water is nobody’s idea of fun – unless you enjoy the crippling pain of ice cream headaches without the pleasure of an actual ice cream cone. At the opposite end of the spectrum, swimming in very warm water can also crater your comfort and results. That’s why we were psyched to test the EZ Hydro-Glide Cap, a one-of-a-kind attempt to boost swimming performance and safety using wearable technology designed to enhance thermoregulation.

In plain English: The Hydro-Glide is a potentially game-changing swim accessory that’s supposed to make you less susceptible to cold shock and heat stress.

Before we dive into the science, an crucial clarification: The critical technology here is not a cap, but a 3D-printed contraption that goes under your cap. More on that below.

But first, kudos to EZ Gains, a popular outside-the-box triathlon retailer, for attacking a problem that numerous triathletes experience – significant discomfort when swimming in very cold and very warm water. We’ve learned a lot in recent years about thermoregulation, and any improvements in this area could help many athletes, including friends of mine who’ve quit the sport after repeated unpleasant swims.

Sources indicate that EZ Gains’ approach is based on credible science. The company notes that your head plays an outsized role in your body’s response to ambient temperatures, given the extensive network of blood vessels and nerves just beneath your scalp. This rings true, as does the contention that regulating the temperature difference between the water and your head – both the initial gap and the ongoing variance – can mitigate the downsides of extreme heat and cold.

According to recent reports, we use insulated neoprene caps for chilly swims, after all. What if a single, more sophisticated solution helped us thrive in both polar and equatorial waters?

In a recent development, EZ Gains’ answer is a honeycombed high-tech foam and hard plastic wedge that sits at the top of your forehead under an (included) standard swim cap. Before putting it on, you can place one or two small thermal packs (also included) inside the hollow center of the wedge. These packs – and an additional thin heating strip – provide a cooling or warming effect as needed. In warm water, you can use a frozen pack or two to cool your forehead, which is meant to keep your core temp down and reduce heat fatigue.

Industry observers note that you’re also supposed to use frozen packs when swimming in frigid water – say 60 degrees F or less – according to EZ Gains. The idea is to pre-condition your head to the chilly temps you’re about to encounter. This may sound counterintuitive, but EZ Gains indicates the pre-cooling technique can prevent cold shock, a serious autonomic response that elevates your heart rate and can cause panic and even cardiac arrest. The packs can also be heated for a touch of warmth when facing cool-but-not-arctic conditions.

For more preparation for swimming in cold water, read: How to Acclimate and Prepare for Cold-Water Triathlons.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the system, I tested it in various bodies of water over the course of five months, from midsummer to late autumn. My primary locations were indoor and outdoor pools in Boulder, Colorado, and our local reservoir. Water temperatures ranged from 84 degrees F all the way down to 50 degrees F. All of my swims were 45-90 minutes long, more than enough to mimic race conditions and assess how well the device limits heat and cold stress.

The TLDR from my testing: Some upcoming technologies sound great on paper but don’t pan out in real life. Sadly, this device is one of those. On two of its three core value propositions, the Hydro-Glide fell short. I’ll tackle them one by one.

First, EZ Gains says the cap will reduce heat fatigue and related complications – anxiety, increased heart rate, dehydration, and confusion – when using the frozen packs. I did notice a cooling sensation in the early parts of my summer swims, typically lasting 10-15 minutes. But while I appreciated the initial cooling, I didn’t discern a material difference in fatigue, judgment, or heart rate after an hour, even during my most intense workouts.

Second, the cap is supposed to prevent the instant discomfort and cold shock that many people experience when diving into frigid water. Perhaps I’m less sensitive than other athletes (my long-suffering wife might have an opinion on this), but using slightly thawed ice packs to pre-cool my head (as instructed) didn’t eliminate the ice cream headaches.

It has been revealed that in my experience, this kind of pain starts in my face and forehead, neither of which are protected by the device. It’s possible that the Hydro-Glide would help other swimmers, since physiological reactions vary widely, but I’d speculate that too much of your face, forehead, and neck remain exposed for the cold to be significantly neutralized.

Industry observers note that third, EZ Gains states the cap will protect your head when another swimmer clobbers you, which seems legit in the case of head-on impacts. A friend in my Masters group sustained a concussion last year when another swimmer swerved into her during a backstroke set. While I didn’t do any head-banging to test this claim, it’s reasonable to believe the Hydro-Glide’s foam would’ve absorbed that blow. Since the wedge doesn’t cover the sides or back of your head, though, it wouldn’t deflect all-too-common errant elbows or kicks to those areas during a race start.

In a recent development, there are two additional downsides to consider. If you have an XL melon like mine, you may experience discomfort from the pressure of the cone against your head. I did, typically after about 30 minutes. And if you’re even the slightest bit fashion-conscious, you will probably draw the line at looking like a Corythosaurus from Jurassic Park. The first time I showed up at the pool wearing the Hydro-Glide, several of my masters teammates burst out laughing. Someone compared me to a Conehead.

Which I could possibly live with if the results had been stellar. However, the Hydro-Glide didn’t deliver a meaningful upside for me versus a standard swim cap. While EZ Gains deserves praise for its waaay-out-of-the-box effort to improve swim safety and comfort, this product’s current execution doesn’t justify a $270 investment.

#22472. The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3928 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

📅 07 Jun 2023 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Sources indicate that there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here.
  • In 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that there are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of new super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

In 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

Here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → Upcoming Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s).

It has been revealed that besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in new shoes marathon morning.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. New shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

All of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

On a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in New York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

In a recent development, the carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

Sources indicate that my only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no problems—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com.

Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review.

According to recent reports, the Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you update a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

The ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

The width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

Industry observers note that the main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Sources indicate that the jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any problems pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

Recent findings suggest that new Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

Latest Balance SuperComp Rebel Review.

Recent findings suggest that the Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

Sources indicate that the source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

Recent findings suggest that the shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

Shop Endorphin Elite 3 at saucony.com.

Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 Review.

It has been revealed that when I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

Recent findings suggest that at the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

In a recent development, the Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

Industry observers note that where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com.

Asics Metaspeed Tokyo Shoes Review.

Altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

Sources indicate that the third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

In a recent development, its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

Recent findings suggest that “What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” remarked tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

Recent findings suggest that “Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

It has been revealed that the lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

Industry observers note that and our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” remarked tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that problem and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”.

Besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

Shop Hoka Cielo X1 3 at hoka.com.

According to recent reports, the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” claims a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

Sources indicate that the shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

Industry observers note that putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” states tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”.

But that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” notes tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”.

Some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

When I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

In a recent development, the shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

Recent findings suggest that I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 Review.

Sources indicate that though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

She gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

Recent findings suggest that still, the new cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

For hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

Industry observers note that another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com.

Sources indicate that brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

Do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An crucial lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

It has been revealed that some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

The secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

Recent findings suggest that while these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:.

In a recent development, A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

Sources indicate that saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.).

“The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” claims Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”.

However, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

According to recent reports, editor’s Note, November 17, 2026: The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is presently our “Best Overall” choice. Recently, the Adrenaline GTS 26 dropped, but we’ve not tested it yet. It’s on the list because we loved the 25 so much. The 25 is currently on sale, so grab it while you can.

In a recent development, some shoes do not have a sexy reputation. Say “stability shoe” to a certain kind of runner and they’ll look like you just suggested they run their next marathon in Crocs. Stability shoes have a reputation problem, and it’s not entirely undeserved. The stability shoes of the early 2000s were clunky, rigid bricks that treated pronation like a disease to be cured with a slab of hard plastic (looking at you, Saucony Grid Azuras). If you ran through that era, I get why you might have a negative, visceral reaction to the type.

Industry observers note that but here’s the thing: Stability shoes got better. Today’s versions are lighter, softer, and not for anything? Cuter. And they are some of the best shoes you can lace up—not just for overpronators, but for anyone whose form gets sloppy when the miles pile up. I’ve known runners who white-knuckle their way through marathon blocks in neutral racers when a little guidance would have saved their knees, their IT bands, and frankly, their sourpusses. Needing support isn’t taking an L. It’s biomechanics.

Industry observers note that at its simplest, a stability shoe is designed to limit excess inward rolling of the foot (overpronation) after your foot strikes the ground. A little pronation is normal and even beneficial; it helps distribute the shock of the impact. But when your ankle collapses too far inward with every step, that torque travels up the chain to your shins, knees, and hips, and over hundreds of miles it can screw up not just your stride, but your long-term health.

Neutral shoes let your foot do whatever it wants. Stability shoes help guide your foot into a more correct placement, keeping your body more aligned.

From pounding the pavement to scrutinizing performance in our Shoe Lab, the Runner’s World test editors and wear-testers rigorously tested all of our selections. Our process includes exhaustive market research, analysis of user feedback, and consultations with industry experts. This article was written jointly between our editors Amanda Furrer and Cat Bowen. Bowen tends to pronate, especially when she is tired or in a long training block. She has run in all the shoes on this list with the exception of the Nike Structure Plus.

The Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is one of the most consistent stability shoes on the market, and the silver anniversary upgrade makes a strong case for why this franchise has lasted 25 years. The big news is in the stack: Brooks added 3 mm to the forefoot and 1 mm to the heel, bringing it to 37 mm and 27 mm respectively, and dropped the heel-to-toe offset from 12 mm down to 10 mm for the first time in the shoe’s history.

The newly introduced heel bevel is the smoothest the Adrenaline has ever had in the opinion of Bowen, who has put serious miles on this shoe. She also feels as though it’s the most balanced this shoe has ever been, and the most balanced on this list.

Recent findings suggest that “Some stability shoes can be so aggressive that the rails can begin to pinch the lateral sides of the foot during long runs,” she claims. “The Adrenaline GTS 25 doesn’t do that, and they still have the cushion and push to power your runs.”.

DNA Loft v3 foam carries over from the 24, but the extra volume makes the ride noticeably softer underfoot, especially at heel strike. Guide rails are still doing their thing on the medial and lateral edges—reactive, not prescriptive, engaging only when your stride asks for it. The upper is a breathable engineered mesh that has the benefit of preventing overheating and swamp foot with a stretch knit heel collar that locks down without overcrowding.

Though it should be noted that some testers, including Courtney Kazmierczak, feel as though the collar is a hair too high in the back, which requires some trial and error for sock choice.

At 10.6 ounces, it’s not light, but it’s not trying to be. This is a daily trainer for runners who want structure and protection. It’s a shoe that simply does not pinch or bite.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Sources indicate that this is not a rebuild or huge design change. This is a fine-tuning. The basics are the same; the Adrenaline GTS 26 still uses guide rails as the support system, it has the same stack height, the same drop, the profile hasn’t changed, and the core of the midsole is still the DNA Loft v3 foam.

What did change is that they made it a little bit more breathable by using an engineered mesh upper. The tongue is a bit flatter for a more tuned-in fit, and the heel collar is more refined with a generous pull-tab, which is great for runners with accessibility or limb differences.

The trade-off here is that it is a teensy bit heavier. We’re talking a few tenths of an ounce difference. And, if I’m being the picky and petty editor that I am? I think the colors and design for this model aren’t as cute. I know, I know, lame thing to bring up, but I really just want a stability shoe in a fun neon. Just because I run like a duck doesn’t mean I don’t deserve fun.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

Industry observers note that these may be our best value pick, but they’re also some of the most durable daily stability trainers on this list. “I like the durability and stability of these shoes and the fact that they are lighter than previous models,” said shoe tester Lauren Woodall. “I am able to put more miles on these shoes before they need to be replaced than other running shoes.”.

The thing is, even though it’s heavier, and the durability is noticeable, they’re not bricks. They are your easy run shoes, your throw-on-and-go trainers. They’re not the fastest, but they’re not meant to be. When your body is tired, and you need the assistance of that wave plate and the heft of the Enerzy NXT foam, it’s there for you like an old friend holding out a hand. The guardrails on this shoe aren’t superpowered corrections like they were on earlier models, but the gentle effectiveness of them cannot be overstated. Simply put, these shoes just feel really good on your run.

Recent findings suggest that one note about fit: a few of our testers found that you can get a bit of heel slippage in these. However, Mizuno gives you that extra eyelet for a heel lock, and that can absolutely change the fit of the shoe once you lace up. It’s a point worth remembering.

Shop Men’s at usa.mizuno.com | Shop Women’s at usa.mizuno.com.

The Arahi 9 is Hoka-soft, but not max-cush beefy. It’s a versatile model that does double duty as an everyday trainer or tempo shoe. The brand made small tweaks to the upper for a better fit, and made them a little bit less expensive as well. It’s not a huge redesign as much as it’s a refinement.

In a recent development, you forget the Arahi 9 is a stability shoe because of how streamlined the design looks: it’s sleek and a compliment magnet. Hoka modified the upper to dial in the fit a bit more, make it a little more breathable, and adjust some of the hot points felt in the 8.

Sources indicate that invisible to the eye is the H-Frame system that keeps you stable. The H-Frame is a dense piece of foam in the midsole that’s H-shaped. The result is surprising; you’d think the H-Frame would make the Arahi rigid and heavy, but instead the shoe is lightweight and the ride is smooth. Running in it, Furrer felt like she was gliding.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com.

Recent findings suggest that there’s something about the Nike Structure Plus that demands attention. In the words of Furrer, “I have a soft spot for this shoe, it’s just so good on long runs.” And that right there is spot on. For the days when you know you have a long run on the calendar, but that long run is full of mixed tempos, hill climbs, potential obstacles, and rough surfaces that you’ll start to feel underfoot after six miles, this is going to be the shoe you reach for. That’s what Nike designed it to handle when it combined the ReactX and ZoomX foams with a dual-zone rubber outsole. It gives you cushion where you need it, flexibility where it matters most, and a nimble feel when you’re dodging pavement cracks.

Arguably the most stylish shoe on this list, Nike really leveled up its stability line with the Structure. It’s also very orthotic-friendly. The collar and the lacing system can handle a lot of pulling, allowing you to get those insoles in correctly. Beyond that, it’s remarkably comfortable as a shoe just to take out and live in. It’s a solid walking shoe, and we love it as a versatile, more cushioned alternative to wear with dressier outfits.

It has been revealed that that’s not to say it’s flawless. It’s a bit on the heavier side, and if you’re someone who prefers a shoe that has a lot of responsiveness or bounce, you won’t find it in this shoe. It’s also just a hair on the “runs smaller” side front to back. But other than those small quibbles, it’s a great pair.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Industry observers note that the differences between the Gel-Kayano 32 and the 33 are vital, but not massive. They retooled the design of the support system, employing their FluidSupport tech, which is a bit more malleable than previous iterations, working more with the body’s movements and mechanics. They’ve also softened the foam, updated the fit throughout, and for many runners, it should feel and ride more comfortably.

That being noted, it still has all the Asics features you expect and love: a breathable upper, geometry that works to move you forward, and a grippy sole that keeps you upright on wet pavement. It is on the heavier side, but nothing out of the ordinary for a stability shoe, and the collar could have a hair more cushion. However, we love the well-placed heel tab, especially when our hands are sweaty.

Sources indicate that the cushion is going to be the biggest win on long-run days. You may not get a ton of energy return, but what you are getting is that added comfort with the guidance that will help you maintain your form and keep you from hating yourself after the run when you’re inevitably lying on the floor propped up on your hands.

Shop Men’s at asics.com |Shop Women’s at asics.com.

According to recent reports, the Saucony Guide 19 is a stability shoe that actually earns the word “versatile,” which stability shoes rarely do. Most of them feel like you’re being guided rather than running, but the Guide 19 threads the needle between structured support and genuine responsiveness.

The foundation is Pwrrun foam, which delivers a cushioned but not marshmallow-soft ride. It’s lively enough to handle tempo work without feeling like you’re fighting the shoe, and cushioned enough that you’re not destroyed after 18 miles. The medial TPU guidance frame offers mild overpronation correction without the brick-like rigidity you get from old-school posts. It’s more a gentle steer rather than having the shoe take the reins and navigate your feet for you.

Industry observers note that for long runs, the 8 mm drop and 32 mm stack height in the heel keep things comfortable for time-on-feet without creating that spongy instability that kills your form late in a run. For daily training, it’s durable and consistent and a shoe you can lace up without thinking too hard about what’s on your schedule.

And it’s just plain comfortable. At least according to our wear-tester Dave Block, who “can’t remember a shoe that’s felt this great.” And even for tempo days on the track, the fit on this shoe just gets it right. It fits snugly enough that at faster paces it doesn’t feel sloppy.It won’t replace a racing flat, but for runners who want one shoe that handles most of their weekly mileage without drama, the Guide 19 makes a strong case.

Shop Men’s at saucony.com |Shop Women’s at saucony.com.

It has been revealed that what separates the Hoka Rocket X 3 from other super shoes is its broader base and accommodating fit. The shoe has a winged carbon plate to help with propulsion and a dual-density PEBA midsole to provide high energy return and supportive cushioning. An vital enhancement: a sticky rubber outsole to prevent slipping and sliding when the race forecast predicts rain or snow.

According to recent reports, “These shoes were very stable, which is different for a racing shoe,” claims tester Shane Houghton, an overpronator. “Most super shoes feel kind wobbly but I felt lower to the ground and never felt in danger of rolling an ankle. When I stand in the shoes I feel flat on my feet and I don’t feel any lateral-rocking. I had no anxiety wearing these during loopy intervals or running around curves. The lacing is tight and like the texture of the ribbed laces. It keeps them from coming undone or loosening while running.”.

Sometimes, shoes that are very much stabilizing or stability-adjacent shirk that term for optics. I can’t prove it, but I believe the Nike ACG Zegamas fit that description.

I’ve spent months running in these, and as someone who pronates frequently, I can tell you they deliver the structure and support of a true stability shoe wrapped in the rugged outsole of a trail runner. It comes down to that revised last. The Zegama cups the outer rim of your foot so thoroughly that it holds you locked in place, correcting the roll before it starts.

Recent findings suggest that the support straps built into the upper wrap all the way around your foot, the padded tongue and lacing lock your midfoot down, and the heel keeps you planted without any slip. It doesn’t feel neutral, but it doesn’t steer you, either. Instead, it almost feels like it’s anticipatory rather than corrective.

Pair that underfoot security with a grippy Vibram outsole and aggressive lugs that bite into mud and wet rock, and you get the best of both worlds—the stable, planted feel of a stability shoe with the traction to handle whatever the trail throws at you.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

Sources indicate that with any piece of running equipment, comfort should be your foremost deciding factor. Here are a few thing to consider before your next shoe fitting:.

1) The shoe should have enough room for your toes to splay in the toebox, about a thumbnail’s width from the front of the shoe to the tip of your longest toe.

2) The shoe shouldn’t feel too tight or loose around the midfoot area. There are lacing techniques to help modify your shoe’s width, but you should also consider different widths instead of the standard D (men) or B (women) width.

Recent findings suggest that 3) A secure heel is also paramount, as slippage can cause blisters. The heel-lock lacing method—threading each lace in the etra eyelet next to it to create a loop, then crisscrossing the opposite laces through the loop to create a “lock”—can give you a more secure fit.

It has been revealed that 4) Give the shoes a run at the store or check website’s return/exchange policies. Besides trying on the shoe, the best way to know if it’s comfy is if you run in it, too.

In a recent development, some runners want maximum cushioning underfoot while others want less padding to experience more ground feel. New foam technology has given us the best of both worlds with plush, high-stacked cushioning that’s lightweight, too. Because of these high stack heights, stability tech is added to help runners run course tangents—and not twist their ankles while doing so.

Still, shoes with thicker cushioning and a high stack (36mm or more) tend to be squishier, making them less stable. Shoes with lower stack heights (32mm or less in the heel) provide a closer-to-the-ground feel and better feedback.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to give up max-cushioning if you’re an overpronator, however. Besides looking for shoes with built-in stability features, like guide rails and stability planes, consider shoes with wide, exaggerated soles, particularly under the heel, and a wider midfoot. Raised sidewalls (the interior padded sides of the shoe) create a snugger fit that will also enhance support, ensuring optimal stability and comfort.

Besides looking for shoes with stability features, you should also consider the type of workouts you’ll be performing in these shoes.

For speedwork, like tempos and track workouts, lightweight trainers (less than 9 ounces for men or 8 ounces for women) with a curved “rocker” midsole help you surge forward. For everyday runs and longer runs, slightly heavier shoes with more padding provide the comfort and durability that you want on a daily training run. Or if you’re interested in venturing off-road, it’s key to have a trail shoe made for rough, undulating terrain.

Do I actually need a stability shoe?

According to recent reports, stability shoes are specifically designed for overpronation, a type of gait pattern when your foot rolls too far inward upon landing. Flat-foot, low arch runners can also benefit from this extra padding in shoes.

Not every flat-foot runner or overpronator may need the extra support, however, especially if their feet only have a slight roll. We strongly advise having your gait evaluated by a professional, such as a podiatrist, physical therapist, or movement specialist. They can confirm if you need motion-specific shoes or an orthotic insert.

The best stability shoes focus on enhancing comfort and promoting a natural gait rather than imposing a harsh, corrective feel. While extra padding may sound like a plus, it can be too prescriptive for some runners. Worst-case scenario: Overcorrecting a neutral stride could increase your chance of injury, rather than make you more comfortable.

If you’re a new runner unsure of your gait pattern, we recommend running in a neutral shoe, like the Hoka Clifton 11s, first.

When should neutral runners consider wearing a stability shoe?

Some shoes with stability tech lend support to late-onset overpronators, i.e., neutral runners whose form becomes erratic midrun due to fatigue. Brands like Brooks and Altra, for instance, use denser foam on the medial and lateral sides of the midsole to help control excessive movement and promote knee and foot alignment, resulting in a more efficient stride.

Is there an adjustment to running in stability shoes?

Recent findings suggest that as with any running shoe transition, like trying zero-drop trainers for the first time, you’ll want to gradually make the switch if you usually wear neutral shoes. Start with shorter runs and then slowly ramp up mileage or runtime as your body adjusts to the upcoming shoes. Read your body for cues; if you feel some discomfort you may need a slower process before fully committing to stability shoes. Muscle fatigue and pain can also be non-shoe-related and be attributed to overuse. If this is not the problem and it is the shoes, discontinue running in them and talk to a specialist for further evaluation.

Do stability shoes “fix” overpronation?

No. Instead, they support your existing gait pattern. Your shoes can make you feel more comfortable and stable, but it doesn’t change that pattern.

According to recent reports, in the words of Test Editor Morgan Petruny: “Keep in mind that a stability shoe is not a cure-all or magic pill. Rather, it is a tool.”.

Industry observers note that overpronation can be due to various factors, including biomechanics, muscle strength, and flexibility, so stability shoes are just one component of a comprehensive approach to managing its negative effects. Strengthening exercises, gait analysis, and proper running form can also play crucial roles in that effort.

Industry News: ‘One of a Million’: She’s 3-Foot-9, Just Ran a 3:42 Marathon, and Is Chasing a Boston Qualifier

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.

According to recent reports, “Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she stated. “For me, my view is hundreds of butts. It’s not the most inspirational view.”.

It’s one difference that Windsor, who is 3-foot-9, has learned to navigate as a runner with dwarfism. But that hasn't stopped her from beating many of those butts in races.

Sources indicate that at the Indianapolis Marathon on November 7, Windsor, 39, ran 3:42:00 to finish in the top third of her 35–39 age group, averaging an 8:28 mile pace. The time was a PR by seven minutes and is provisionally a new American record for the T40 para category (a division for athletes with short stature).

Industry observers note that windsor was born with an extremely rare form of dwarfism called acromesomelic dysplasia. “Last I heard, I’m one of a million,” remarked Windsor, who works as a physician assistant in developmental pediatrics.

It has been revealed that windsor’s run in Indianapolis is more impressive considering that this is part two of her marathoning career. After taking a decade off to raise her two kids in 2014, Windsor has come back even stronger, knocking off more than an hour from her pre-hiatus personal best.

Sources indicate that “I just think the human body is just such an amazing thing,” she noted. “And that when asked something difficult of it, what you’re capable of doing can sometimes be really surprising.”.

As a middle schooler, Windsor joined the track team to hang out with her friends and went in with low expectations. But that changed when she beat another runner in an 800-meter race. It was motivating, and Windsor eventually realized that although she couldn’t dust her peers in a sprint, she had exceptional grit and endurance. “I might not be able to outrun them, but I could outlast them,” she remembers.

Sources indicate that in her twenties, Windsor set her sights on the marathon—and one marathon in particular. She wanted to become the first person with dwarfism to run the prestigious Boston Marathon. In 2013, her dream almost came true, but as she neared the finish line on Boylston Street, she was forced to stop. Terrorists had detonated bombs at the finish. Windsor was unharmed, but her dream would have to wait.

The next year, Windsor became the first person with dwarfism to complete the historic race, running 4:43:26. That would be her last marathon for a decade, as Windsor raised two kids and focused on her family.

In 2025, she felt pulled back to the distance. She signed up for the Spinx Marathon in Greenville, South Carolina, where she ran 4:09:51—more than 30 minutes faster than her personal best from Boston.

Not long after, Windsor started working with coach Esther Atkins, a former professional marathoner who coaches with McKirdy Trained. Atkins saw potential in Windsor and had a hunch she could run a lot faster. While unsure at first, Windsor was assuaged when she nabbed another massive personal best, running 3:49:42 at the 2026 Boston Marathon in April.

Atkins, who works with about 40 athletes, is impressed by how coachable Windsor is. “She’s always open to trying something different, and very eager to push the boundaries of what she has done before or what she has believed she was capable of,” Atkins said.

“I’m not used to people expecting more of me than I expect of myself; usually it’s the other way around,” Windsor said. “And that’s how I know I have an exceptional coach. She sees the possibilities and isn’t stumped by my unique challenges.”.

As a runner with dwarfism, Windsor is presented with obstacles that most runners don’t face. Her cadence, for example, is much higher than the average runner. While 180 steps per minute is a commonly cited target among runners, Windsor averaged 207 steps per minute at Indianapolis, and because her stride length is much shorter, she covers less ground per step. (For reference, Windsor is about the height of an average 6-year-old.).

In a recent development, windsor also has to navigate crowds carefully—she doesn’t always show up in the peripheral vision of competitors. She generally runs on the right side of the road to improve her visibility and avoid getting tripped up or surprising people as she passes. At larger races, like Boston or Indy, she is able to start a few minutes ahead of the masses to let the race string out.

And then there are shoes. Windsor wears a kids’ size 13, but it’s hard to find athletic shoes in her size that aren’t Velcro or light-up. She generally sizes up to a size 1 for running shoes and uses custom orthotics. But such small sizes don’t have the bells and whistles of normal running shoes. And super shoes that small don’t exist.

Industry observers note that so far, Windsor has liked Asics the best. “I don’t think I fully appreciated the difference of having a good quality shoe until I tried [an Asics shoe] on,” she noted. “And even just having a gel cushion was like, ‘Is this how everybody else feels? This is what I've been missing out on.’”.

Windsor ran Indianapolis in the GT-2000, although they’re still a little pared down compared to a mass-market adult shoe. “I really wish there were better options and better technology, because I've had to just work with what my options are,” she remarked.

Until recently, Windsor wasn’t able to find a GPS watch that fit her wrists. Last summer, she discovered that Garmin made a 42mm watch, which finally allowed her to run without a phone and gave her insights like cadence and stride length. She partially credits the data for her recent improvement.

In a recent development, looking ahead, Windsor has two goals. The first is to qualify for Boston in her age group. Windsor has already nabbed a BQ in the adaptive athlete field, but she’s targeting the able-bodied BQ. She turns 40 next spring, which will bump her to the 40–44 age group. She’ll need to run under 3:35:00—about 7 minutes faster than her personal best—to achieve the standard.

In a recent development, her other goal is to create more opportunities for runners in her Paralympic category. Currently, World ParaAthletics doesn’t sanction running events in the short stature division. USATF recently began to include the marathon in the T40 category, a record which Windsor owns. But the record book isn’t what drives her.

In a recent development, “It's less about competition, more about just setting some sort of a standard, and that records are meant to be broken …” she said. “I would love for to open up opportunities for people to at least be curious and give it a try.”.

In a recent development, next up for Windsor? The Tokyo Marathon on March 7—one week before her 40th birthday.

Theo Kahler is the senior news editor at Runner’s World. He’s a former all-conference collegiate runner at Winthrop University, and he received his master’s degree in liberal arts studies from Wake Forest University, where he was a member of one of the top distance-running teams in the NCAA. Kahler has reported on the ground at major events such as the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials, Newly introduced York City Marathon, and Boston Marathon. He’s run 14:20 in the 5K, 1:05:37 in the half marathon, and finished 40th at the 2025 New York City Marathon. He enjoys spotting tracks from the sky on airplanes. (Look for colorful ovals around football fields.).

#22467. After 50 Years of Running, I’m Facing My Toughest Challenge: Having to Let Go of the Runner I Used to Be

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)
